Preface: This work, titled *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, was composed by the illustrious Hemādri, a great teacher (*mahāmahopādhyāya*) and an ornament of the scholarly community whose fame is widely renowned. He was indeed born in the southern region (*dākṣiṇātyajanapada*).
From the best of the twice-born named Kāmadeva, who belonged to the Vātsa lineage, were born Vāsudeva and Vāmanadeva;

these were, respectively, his grandfather and great-grandfather. Hemādri, however, was the son of Mahādeva Sūri, the lord of the city of Devagiri, a preeminent ornament of the Yādava dynasty whose name was widely renowned, and the sovereign of all Karṇāṭaka.
There was a scholar named Hemādri. That king ascended the throne in the year measured by the [Śaka] era as eight hundred and ninety-nine (899). Hemādri was indeed a contemporary of him.
His *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* consists of the sections on Vows (*Vrata-khaṇḍa*), Gifts (*Dāna-khaṇḍa*), Sacrifices (*Sautrāmaṇī-khaṇḍa*), and Liberation (*Mokṣa-khaṇḍa*).

It is complete with the five members, including the conclusion (*śeṣa*) and the refutation (*khaṇḍa*). Among these, the portion up to the vow (*vrata*) has been printed with the permission of the Honorable President of the Asiatic Society of Bengal and through the editorial efforts of the illustrious Paṇḍita Bharatacandra Śiromaṇi. Following that—

This work has been printed through the efforts of the purification undertaken by the two of us, at the request of the honorable Śrī Kālasara-vanājādhyakṣa Mahodaya, who belongs to the Śrāddha-khaya within the Parishēṣa-khanda of the Mahā-indiyāṇā lineage.

The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess any dharma by which he is designated as 'Tathāgata'? Subhūti replied: "As I understand the meaning of the Blessed One’s teaching, there is no dharma whatsoever by which the Tathāgata is designated as 'Tathāgata'. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma at all that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to? Subhūti replied: "No indeed, Blessed One, there is not. Why is that? Because that dharma which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to is ineffable, unutterable, and beyond all conceptualization. It cannot be expressed by words; it is neither a dharma nor a non-dharma. The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is so. It is exactly as you have said. Subhūti, the dharma which the Tathāgata has fully awakened to is ineffable, unutterable, and beyond all conceptualization. It cannot be expressed by words; it is neither a dharma nor a non-dharma. Therefore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata designates this dharma as 'the dharma of a Tathāgata. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, how does the Tathāgata designate this dharma as 'the dharma of a Tathāgata'? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, because that dharma is neither a dharma nor a non-dharma, therefore the Tathāgata designates it as 'the dharma of a Tathāgata. Subhūti, if there were any dharma whatsoever by which the Tathāgata were designated as 'Tathāgata,' then the Dharma-body would be grasped, and the Tathāgata would grasp a dharma. ... : [The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, it is as if there were a great banyan tree standing at the crossroads. Its roots would extend for a yojana, its trunk for a yojana, and its branches and foliage would spread for a yojana on all sides. Suppose a man were to come along who was desirous of seeing that great banyan tree. He would approach from the east, and having approached, he would see the great banyan tree from the east. Having seen it, he would think: ‘This great banyan tree is vast, extensive, and magnificent. Then he would approach from the south, the west, and the north, and having approached from each direction, he would see the great banyan tree from that direction. Having seen it, he would think: ‘This great banyan tree is vast, extensive, and magnificent. In the same way, Ānanda, when a noble disciple has abandoned the five lower fetters, he is called one who has attained parinirvāṇa in the interval.”

... : : 126. The Blessed One said this: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? They are: the person who is like a lotus flower, the person who is like a blue lotus flower, the person who is like a white lotus flower, and the person who is like a fragrant lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction, and likewise toward the second, the third, and the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable, and free from enmity and ill will. He dwells with a mind full of compassion toward one direction, and likewise toward the second, the third, and the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with compassion—vast, exalted, immeasurable, and free from enmity and ill will. He dwells with a mind full of sympathetic joy toward one direction, and likewise toward the second, the third, and the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy—vast, exalted, immeasurable, and free from enmity and ill will. He dwells with a mind full of equanimity toward one direction, and likewise toward the second, the third, and the fourth; thus above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, and free from enmity and ill will. Just as a blue, red, or white lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and stands unsoiled by the water; even so, monks, that person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction... [and so on for the other three immeasurables] ...thus above, below, across, everywhere, and in all respects, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, and free from enmity and ill will. [The Venerable Ānanda said: “What is meant by the ‘greatness of the mental disposition’? The Blessed One replied: “It refers to the fact that they generate a mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings. [The Venerable Ānanda said: “What is meant by the ‘greatness of the equipment’? The Blessed One replied: “It refers to the fact that they gather the two accumulations of merit and wisdom over three incalculable eons. [The Venerable Ānanda said: “What is meant by the ‘greatness of the time’? The Blessed One replied: “It refers to the fact that they remain for three incalculable eons until they attain unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. [The Venerable Ānanda said: “What is meant by the ‘greatness of the wisdom’? [The Venerable Ānanda said: “What is meant by the ‘greatness of the liberation’? The Blessed One replied: “It refers to the fact that they attain the unobstructed liberation of the Tathāgatas, which is free from all conceptual proliferation. “Ānanda, because it is endowed with these seven kinds of greatness, this Dharma discourse is called the ‘Great Vehicle. Although such a work as this, being without beginning or end, is indeed unlimited, nevertheless—

Limitation is established through the activities of the planets, such as the sun, which possess beginnings and ends; because those activities— like the continuum of seeds and sprouts— are without beginning or end, it is possible for even time, though itself beginningless and endless, to be delimited by them.
And so it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"O twice-born ones, although its size is exceedingly subtle and yet vast,
the measurement of that [universe] is to be known by the wise according to the movement of the planets."
Likewise, time (*kāla*), which is determined through such perceptible actions as the blinking of the eyes by people like us, has been explained in that very same place:
"A *mātrā* equal to the duration of one's own syllable is proclaimed to be a *nimeṣa*."
Therefore, a time even subtler than that is not perceived by the mind.

Just as a substance is not perceived when broken down into its atoms, so too, two *nimeṣas* (twinklings of an eye) should be known as a *truṭi*; ten *truṭis* are traditionally said to constitute one *prāṇa*.
Six breaths (prāṇas) constitute one nāḍikā, and sixty such nāḍikās are traditionally known as an ahorātra; this is indeed proclaimed to be the eternal measure.
O Rāma, thirty muhūrtas are said to constitute a day and night;
of these, fifteen are always proclaimed to be active during the day.
O mighty-armed one, as the sun gradually ascends toward the northern direction, so too does the length of the day increase.
Just as the day attains an increase according to its course,
so too is the increase of those who rely upon it proclaimed.
O Rāma, as the days increase, so too does the loss of wealth;
thus it is stated in the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, in the section on the determination of time within the *Parīśeṣa-khaṇḍa*.
The loss of the sons residing therein should be understood to correspond exactly to that [loss].
The sun traverses four pādas of the zodiac in succession;
one should understand that the decrease of the day is exactly to that same extent.
Upon its waning, however, it is drunk by him; likewise,
when the thousand-rayed sun enters his own [orb], Rādhā, who is dependent upon him, increases accordingly.
The time from sunrise to sunset is designated by the term "viṣuvat."

[1.80] And thus, that solar activity which is delimited by the time of activities such as the blinking of an eye— when two such activities constitute parts of another activity, that [other] activity is delimited by them.

Time becomes the object of the conventional usage "one's own day. In this same way, other conventions such as breaths (*prāṇa*) and *vināḍikās* are to be understood; thus, by means of the movement of the breath, a day and night (*ahorātra*) is produced. And that [day and night] is shown to be of three kinds in the *Brahmasiddhānta*.
A solar day (sāvana) is the period from sunrise to sunrise;
a lunar day (tithi), however, is one-thirtieth of a solar revolution, which constitutes the duration of the moon's transit.
In the Viṣṇudharmottara, the day and night (ahorātra) is shown to be fourfold:
the lunar day (tithi) is proclaimed as the solar day in the lunar measurement,
and by one such day and night, the solar day (sāvana-divasa) is remembered.
A solar day is said to be by means of the Sun's enjoyment of its portion;
a lunar day (nākṣatra) is traditionally taught to be by means of the Moon's enjoyment of the constellations.

The calculation of the lunar day (tithi) and its divisions has been shown in that very [work]. O Bhārgava, whenever there is a demarcation of time by means of the motions of the moon and the sun, I shall then explain it for those two based upon their motion.

By means of the entire Bhagala [system], the twelve zodiac signs (rāśis) are to be known.
O Rādhā, when the moon is at twenty degrees [of its course], it is called *abhīṣaṅga*;

Also in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa*:
"O Goddess, the Great Kalā is said to be a sixteenth part of a *māṣa*;

O fair-faced one, those very digits of the moon from the new moon (śrama) to the full moon (paurṇamāsī),
numbering sixteen, are declared to be the lunar days (tithis).
In this way, the month has also been shown by the Grandfather (Brahmā) to be of three kinds:

the lunar month (cāndra), characterized by the appearance and disappearance [of the moon], consists of thirty days; the solar month (sāvana), however, consists of thirty [civil] days; and the solar month (saura) is also declared to be that which is marked by the sun's transit (saṃkrānti) through a zodiacal sign.

Regarding the phrase "from the new moon" (*darśāt*), the fifth case ending is used with the elision of the suffix *kha*; thus, the meaning is "after the new moon," starting from the day following the new moon until the end of the *amāvāsyā*.
Accordingly, it has been stated in the *Brahmasiddhānta*:
The lunar month, beginning with the first day of the bright fortnight and ending with the new moon, consists of thirty solar days;
for as long as the sun remains within a single zodiac sign, that duration is known as a *sabhāskara* (solar) month.
The fourfold month has been thus demonstrated by me:
the first is the *sāvana* month, the second is said to be the lunar (*cāndra*) month,
the third is the sidereal (*nākṣatra*) month, and the fourth is the solar (*saura*) month.

In each successive lunar day (tithi), by means of twelve parts,
the moon is joined with the sun at the end of the dark fortnight.
Starting from one conjunction of the moon and sun, and continuing through subsequent conjunctions, that which is designated by the wise as the "lunar month" (cāndra-māsa) is defined.
In the *sāvana* month, thirty sunrises are traditionally reckoned;
the solar month is proclaimed by the Sun’s transit through a zodiacal sign;
and the lunar month is said to be defined by the revolution of all the constellations (*nakṣatras*).
The lunar month (*cāndra*) has been shown by the author of the *Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana* to be of two kinds according to regional convention:
the one beginning with the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣādi*) and the one beginning with the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇādi*). Some, however, do not accept the month that begins with the dark fortnight.
Even those who desire [to go] do not wish to go south of the Vindhya mountains.
And thus it is heard in the Taittirīyaka:

"Having completed the months with the New Moon sacrifice, they omit a day, for they will complete the months with the New Moon sacrifice; having completed the months with the Full Moon sacrifice, they omit a day, [for they will complete them] with the Full Moon sacrifice."
For it is said that [the rites] will be accomplished within the months;

likewise, because those learned in grammar have stated in another *Mahāvārttika* that "the full moon (*pūrṇamāsa*) is in this [month]," the *śrāddha* should be performed day by day during the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja.
And because of this illustration;
for this very reason, in order to grasp the two kinds of lunar months, [it is said]: "In whichever month, on whichever day...
10. [Section on] the determination of the application of specific rites according to the particular month within the year. 11.
That which arises at the end [of a cycle] is to be understood as the month pertaining to occasional (naimittika) rites.

Thus, it has been stated in general that the end of the lunar fortnight (*parvan*) is determined even by the *vyatīpāta* yoga. Furthermore, the occasional rite (*naimittika*) is said to be the annual (*pratisāṃvatsarika*) one, and for the annual rite, the lunar month alone is prescribed, according to the statement:
"In the annual Śrāddha and in rites for the ancestors, the lunar month is praised."
The number of months and days according to the various measures is shown in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"In the [lunar] measure, a month consists of twenty-seven days;
in the remaining measures, a month consists of thirty days."

Some maintain that the word *māsa* should be understood as denoting all four months mentioned above, just like polysemous words such as *go* (cow) and others. Others, however, say: "The word *māsa* refers specifically to the lunar month; [as it is said], 'A year consists of thirteen months,' and 'There exists a thirteenth month.'"

Since Vedic usage—such as "the gods are worshipped every half-month" and "offerings are made to the ancestors month after month"—refers to the lunar month (*cāndra*), that [lunar month] possesses primary significance in all instances, just like the words *yava* (barley) and *varāha* (boar). As Amarasimha states: "The two fortnights, bright and dark, constitute a month."

Not because of its designation; otherwise, one would have designated it as a "lunar month" (*cāndramāsa*). Thus, it has been established that among other designations, the word "month" (*māsa*) refers specifically to the lunar month. Furthermore, this is supported by the designation in the *Purāṇas* and other texts stating, "A month consists of two fortnights. Nor is there a commonality of being "solar" (*mākhavatva*) that persists throughout the four months [of the season].

It is said that [the moon] "moves" (*nubhrayate*) or "arises" (*upapadyate*); however, its application within a month is established through another mode of derivation. Thus, due to the fear of the manifold meanings of the root *kṛp* (to move), the word *māsa* (month) is primarily derived from the moon (*candra*). Regarding this, some say that words such as Caitra and Vaiśākha denote the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) beginning with Citrā and Viśākhā, respectively.
The designation of months as being joined with a specific constellation on the full moon day is according to the instruction of Pāṇini, as it has been stated:

"A time joined with a constellation [is expressed by the word for that constellation], and [the suffix -aṇ] is applied when the name is 'that full moon day in which [it occurs]' (Pāṇini 4.2.3). Here, "joined with a constellation" means joined with any one such as Viśākhā; the full moon day thus joined receives the designation of Vaiśākha and so forth.
12. *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, Section on Supplements (*pariśeṣakhaṇḍa*), Chapter on the Determination of Time (*kālanirṇaya*).

There is no desire for conjunction with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra-yoga*), but rather the reason for its designation is even by a single part; and so it is said in the *Śaṅkaragītā*: "When there is a connection with a lunar mansion, [it is designated] by even a quarter, a half, or a māṣa [of the moon]."
Even when joined with half a lunar day, that [lunar day] which is reversed is not so again.

That month in which that full moon occurs is designated by terms such as Vaiśākha; the use of the suffix -aṇ here (in Vaiśākha) establishes its status as a conventional term (*rūḍhiśabda*) according to the rule "in the sense of a name" (*saṃjñāyām*). Thus says Yavana:

Anyopānya and Tribha are to be known [as occurring] in Phālguna; O Lord, Caitra is considered [to be] Bhibha. The remaining months are to be known as Dvibha, according to the arrangement beginning with Chaitrika.
Also in the *Marṣaṇakāṇḍa*:

"The months beginning with Caitra are to be known as occurring when the moon is conjoined with two, two, and [the rest] of the stars beginning with Citrā; [these are determined] by groups of three, ending in six and seven."

Therefore, because of the conjunction with the Viśākhā and other asterisms, the names "Vaiśākha" and so forth are derived; thus, the conjunction with the lunar mansions (*nakṣatrayoga*) is to be respected. And so says Viṣṇu: "If the month of Māgha is joined with the Madhā [Maghā] asterism, and if Vaiśākha is joined with the Viśākhā asterism. As for that which was stated by the commentator regarding the name "Pauṣa" being due to the conjunction with Puṣya, and so on—

His intention is that this [compound] is not a derivative meaning based on its constituent parts (*suptāvayavārtha*)—as in the case of *aśvakarṇa* and other such words—but rather, like *udbhid* and others, it has some basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) established in some way or another, for the sake of easy understanding by his disciples.
Even the grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*) of the base and suffix is like that of the word *go*, as in "from the root *gam* with the suffix *ḍo*. *Gaccha*...

It should be understood as being like the expression "the cow bellows. Consequently, there is no room for the introduction of such conceptual constructions as: that the word *vaiśākha* refers to the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), or the constellation (*nakṣatra*), or the conjunction with it, or the time associated with it, or the leading forth (*nayana*) on the full moon day, or the full moon day joined with that [constellation], or the conjunction with that; for this is well-established by scripture (*āgama*).
Because it is untenable for words such as "vaiśākhī" and "aśvakarṇa" to denote the genus (*jāti*), they are therefore [words denoting] substances (*dravya*).
9. Determination of the application of specific [lunar] days within the specific divisions of the year:
The words *vaiśākha* and so forth denote the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) conjoined with its respective lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), as stated [in the scriptures];
furthermore, they denote the lunar month (*cāndramāsa*) beginning from the first day (*pratipad*) up to the new moon (*darśa*), which has that specific lunar mansion in its middle.
[The opponent] says: "It is not so. How then is the application of terms such as Vaiśākha and so forth established in the solar month?

For there too, popular usage (*prasiddhi*) prevails. Regarding this, some say: "Because it would involve the fault of assuming multiple [meanings] and so forth. Indeed, among the learned, the application of words such as Vaiśākha is well-established in reference to the lunar month.

O Śāla-lā, in the month of saura, there is no [application of] the scripture; nor is the scriptural usage well-known in common worldly practice, since it is established even as a secondary (gauṇa) sense. And thus it has been said: "Scriptural usage is stronger than comprehension because it is the cause of that [comprehension]; but worldly comprehension is secondary."
"Even by her, one is carried away."
That is incorrect, because there is no distinction regarding the beginning [of the month]. Thus says Gārgya:
"In matters such as the solar month, marriage, and the like, and in sacrifices, the *sāvana* month is inherently [used];
however, for annual rites and ancestral ceremonies (*piṇḍakārya*), the lunar month is recommended."
Vṛhaspati says that Varāhamihira declared the month of saura-mārgaśīrṣa to yield great success in marriage;
Parāśara declares it to be caitra, while pauṣa is said to bestow misfortune.
"The four months beginning with Āṣāḍha are not distinguished [as distinct seasons] by some twice-born ones," and so forth.
According to Baudhāyana:
when Hari is asleep in Cancer, during the month of Āśvina when Indra’s banner is raised,
one should awaken the Goddess in Libra, and Janārdana in Capricorn.
That month is to be known as Āṣāḍha; and Acyuta lies down during Śrāvaṇa.

Therefore, Baudhāyana and others employ terms such as Śrāvaṇa and so forth for the solar month; thus, even today, there is a general consensus regarding this. However, according to the scripture, the metaphorical application (*gauṇī*) pertaining to the solar month is not specifically intended here.
Determination of Time (*Kālanirṇaya*) in the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*.

[1.1] It is established that because of the force of common usage (*prasiddhiprābalyāt*), there is no contradiction with the various conceptual constructions regarding words such as "rice-gruel" (*kṛsara*). Indeed,
the conventional meaning (*prasiddhi*) of the word *vaiśākha* and so forth for the month of *sauramāsa* is accepted by everyone, from cowherds to women.

However, for some, [the term] refers to the lunar month. Therefore, it is established that the words *vaiśākha* and so forth primarily denote solar-lunar months. That is incorrect; for although both [solar and lunar] are well-known and there is no difference in their scriptural authority, the application of the terms *vaiśākha* and so forth is more natural (*sācika*) in the case of the lunar month.

In the month of saura, however, it is not so powerful; as for the fact that in the saura month [Vaiśākha] is preceded by cowherds and women, and that for some it is known by the term *cāndra* (lunar), that too is merely false, because the opposite is actually observed. And thus Pāṇini [says]: "By means of a nakṣatra..."

The term *paurṇamāsī* is applied to that time [in which the moon is full] according to the rule *saṃjñāyām*. Furthermore, there is no such designation for the solar and civil months; therefore, words such as *Caitra* and *Vaiśākha* refer exclusively to lunar months. Seasons (*ṛtu*), however, consist of two months according to both the solar and lunar reckonings. Among these, the solar—

Regarding the *māna* (measurement), it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "O Rāma, two solar months (*sauramāsa*) are designated as a *turi*. Regarding the lunar measurement (*cāndramāna*), it is also stated in the *Trikaṇḍamaṇḍana*.
One should perform all rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti during the lunar months;
in their absence, however, one should follow the solar months—this is the opinion of the astronomers.
Furthermore, the fact that the moon is the cause [of the seasons] is understood from the mantra:
"Another, ordaining the seasons, is born again. Thus it is said.

The first [alternative] is not tenable, because it contradicts the many general statements previously cited, such as: "It must be performed in that very lunar mansion (*rāśi*)," "One should perform it in that very [month]," and "That indeed is its month, and that indeed is its day. [Furthermore, regarding the claim that] "it should be performed even in a *mala-māsa*,"...

The word found in the statement of Paiṭhīnasi is also applicable in this way: when the thirteenth month is a pure (śuddha) one, then that annual rite (*sāṃvatsarika*) should be performed; and when the thirteenth month is an intercalary (*malamāsa*) one, then it should be performed there as well. This is so even because of the contradiction with the plural statements cited previously.
The word "eva" (only) will have its meaning [restricted] to a single instance, because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of it applying to all [instances].

Alternatively, if it is argued that by considering other scriptural statements one [rite] is said to be performed in an intercalary month (*malamāsa*) while another is said to be performed in a pure (*śuddha*) month, then by that very consideration, the scope [of the rule] would be restricted solely to the subject of monthly rites (*māsika*). Nor...

As for the second [position], it is because of the reason already stated, and because of the statement of the *Laghuhārīta-smṛti* which will be cited: "Every year, on the twelfth month. Furthermore, if it is argued that the *śrāddha* should be performed even when there is no solar transit (*asaṃkrānta*)—on account of the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "it should be performed even when there is no transit"—and thus the *śrāddha* is said to be performed in both cases, then [one might ask]: having performed one annual *śrāddha* during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), should it be performed again later?

If performed then, it would not be the first-year anniversary rite (*prathamābdika*). When the thirteenth month becomes pure, then— [as stated] in the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, *Pariccheda* on the Determination of Time (*Kālanirṇaya*) [150]:
In that regard, the first duty is as follows: when the month remembered [for the anniversary] becomes the thirteenth without an intercalary month (*asaṃkrānta*), then it should be performed there;
for this is also supported by the occurrence of the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even so.
Others, however, read: "Since one should not perform the first annual rite (*ābdika*) in a year joined with an intercalary month (*matiyuta*)."
Sudācarya explains it thus, taking *malimluca* as the subject:
"If the first annual anniversary (*prathamābdika*) of one who has died during an intercalary month (*maliṣu*) falls within that same intercalary month, one should not perform it;
for at the time of that first annual anniversary, an intercalary month is impossible. Indeed, in the third year, another intercalary month occurs distinct from the previous intercalary month."
Therefore, for one who has died, the first anniversary and subsequent rites never occur during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*);

thus, the first half of the verse is a restatement of a constant rule (*nityānuvāda*). When, as time passes, the first annual anniversary (*prathamābdika*) of the deceased falls again during that same intercalary month, then in that very [month]...

The meaning is that one should perform the annual *śrāddha* prescribed for the deceased on the anniversary of their death, even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*). "The annual *śrāddha* which is performed every year—
that annual *śrāddha* is not postponed, even in the case of a death occurring in an intercalary month."
The first half of this [verse] refers to the *mālika* (monthly) *amṛta* (nectar-offering) rite; "the annual" (*sāṃvatsara*) refers to the first-year anniversary rite;

"it should not be omitted" (*na varkheta*) means it should not be interrupted; "even in the intercalary month" (*uḍḍe'pi māse*) is merely a reiteration (*anuvāda*). This [interpretation] is incorrect, because a purposeless and constant reiteration is illogical, as it would result in the futility of the grief [expressed]. Therefore:

"The first annual rite (*ābdika*) should be performed during *mala-māsa*"; such is the reading seen in many texts, which is appropriate. Furthermore, the statement "it should not be performed in *mala-māsa*" is consistent with this very meaning.
Therefore, when a *mala-māsa* occurs, the annual rite for one who has died during that month should be performed in that very month. Śramaṇa...
It is established that the first anniversary (*prathamābdika*) is for one who has died within a month. Now this is considered:

even when an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) falls in the interval, should the first anniversary be performed in the thirteenth month, or only when the intercalary month itself becomes the thirteenth? Regarding this, some say: "Even when an intercalary month falls in the interval..."
This statement is intended to mean that the first-anniversary rite (*prathamābdika*) must be performed on the day of death during the month of *payoda*.
As Hārīta said:
"The sons must perform the piṇḍakriyā every year in the twelfth month, [placing] the rice-ball upon a seat made of a maṇa-measure of grain."
In some cases, there may even be thirteen [syllables], but the first must be short while the subsequent one is long.

*Picchakriyā* refers to the funeral rites for the deceased; it is performed when twelve months have elapsed, meaning up until the thirteenth month, or if there is an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) within that year, when fourteen months have elapsed, meaning up until the fifteenth month. This constitutes the annual anniversary rite (*ābdika*).
The meaning is that even in a year containing an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*), the rite should be performed in the twelfth month;

it should not be performed in the thirteenth month. That [interpretation] is incorrect, for if the meaning were "in some year containing an intercalary month," then [the rite] would have to be performed immediately after the subsequent intercalary month, starting from Kārttika.
If the first anniversary (*prathamābdika*) were to fall on the thirteenth lunar day (*māci*) of the month of Āśvina,
the statement of Vyāsa— “On whatever day one dies in the bright fortnight, they know that his annual [śrāddha] should likewise be performed on that same day”—
would be contradicted. However, if the meaning of the word *kvacit* (in some cases) is intended to refer to the thirteenth day, [then there is no contradiction].
In that case, it would be more appropriate to say that there is no contradiction with this statement by way of simultaneous observation (*sahopalakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, if one accepts the secondary meaning (*gauṇārtha*) of the statement "every year on the twelfth month," then the Vedic authority (*śruti*) is established precisely on the basis of the root text: "Whatever desire one may have, the first annual rite (*ābdika*) must be performed on the second day. Thus, [the objection] does not hold.

The assumption of an intervening month (*mūcāntara*) would also fall away in your own position. Thus, first of all, since this is established by the fact that there is no reduction [of months] from the statement, "In every year, in the twelfth month," what was previously stated is now addressed by way of an objection: [the discussion of] the beginning of Kārttika and other [intervening] months.

When the month of Āśvina occurs as an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) and a *śrāddha* is being performed, there is a contradiction with the scriptural statement: "In the three months beginning with Māgha. Since the rites for the ancestors (*paitṛka*) are prescribed for the [regular] month, even if an intercalary month occurs within that year, the rites for the ancestors should indeed be performed in both [the regular and the intercalary] months. Furthermore, the *Pitṛmedhasūtra* states: "If an intercalary month falls, one should perform the ancestral rites in both months. Thus, the ancestral rites must be performed in both.
On the day of the entry of the measurement, one obtains the annual measure for me; it is thus ordained.
The fourth [chapter], consisting of reflection, on the remainder of the desire realm. [150]

"An individual alone might perform [the rite] on the same day, because of the statement 'in some cases' (*kva-cit*); thus, this refers to a case other than that [of the group]. Furthermore, in the alternative case where there is no such [group], the specific distinction is that the fault arises from the pride of ownership regarding the thirteen items. Moreover, the status of the *śrāddha* [is established] simultaneously—"

Is it performed simultaneously or sequentially? First, it cannot be simultaneous, because there would be no room for the performance of another rite within the interval of one rite, and if it were in another context, there would be the fault of three separate sentences.
In the case of the first alternative, [the question arises] whether it is once or repeatedly; in the second case as well, is it the monthly rite or the annual rite that comes first? No.

Firstly, there would be the undesirable consequence of subverting the annual [śrāddha] performed at the specific time following the month; for if it were restricted to another occasion, the same resolution [of the conflict] would apply. Nor is it the case that it subverts the monthly [śrāddha], for the reason already stated.
Furthermore, because of the prescription of the monthly and the subsequent annual rites, even the subversion of that [monthly rite] would result; therefore, it must have another scope.
Furthermore, in your position, there would be the establishment of four statements, whereas in our position, there is only one; thus, there is a great distinction.

Now, [one might argue] that by the statement of Satyavrata, "And if an intercalary month should occur during the increase of the *sava*, then the twelfth [month] would become more than what is required," there are thirteen...
If it is argued that the *māsika* [offering] is prescribed for every month and therefore there is no fault here, it is replied:

by such statements as “in the case of the *saṃvatsara-viddha* and the *pratimāsa*, the *māsika* [is performed],” an option (*vikalpa*) is established regarding the prescription of the *māsika* for every month; consequently, during the thirteen months, the *māsika* is performed every month.

It should be noted that the aforementioned fault applies to the *guṭhāna* [calculation] as well. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in the twelfth month every year," the meaning—that it refers to the twelfth month when an intercalary month occurs—must be described by reflecting upon the entire context of the sentence concerning the creation of months, fortnights, and days. Consequently, this sentence [remains] without contradicting the fast (*upavāsa*).

In that case, the contradiction regarding the cow and the goat would be logical. Furthermore, the following statement from the *Jyotiṣavedāṅga* is also contradicted: "On whichever day the moon and sun are seen together, that should be known as the end of the lunar phase (*parvānta*) for the sake of occasional rites (*naimittika*).
Thus, even the scriptural authority is subverted. What more can be said?

Since the determination of what ought and ought not to be done by a leader on the path of the virtuous is the subject at hand, this section concerning the determination of the *māna* (pride) belonging to the current topic follows.

This statement would be [consistent], for even in a year containing an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) according to your position, it is likewise appropriate because of the determination of the purpose of the other month; this is another distinction. Furthermore, as for those who say...

If one were to perform the *śrāddha* there every year during the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) of Phālguna, the injunction "every year" would be contradicted because there is no distinction between years [in that case]. Furthermore, since it would not occur in the second [year], the universal rule (*vyāpti*) of "every year" would be sublated.
Others, however, explain this as avoiding the aforementioned defects, but they do not maintain that [the *śrāddha*] occurs even after twelve months have passed.

"When [the father] has died, however, it should be performed every month for a year"—this is the injunction. The phrase "beginning with the first" means that this rule applies starting from the second year onwards. For in this way, there is no contradiction with any of the scriptures. Otherwise, [the practice] would be established differently by means of specific Smṛti texts regarding the months.
Because it would lead to a contradiction that the first year’s [śrāddha] would have to be performed in the second [lunar month],

it should be understood that when the thirteenth month occurs, the first annual śrāddha (prathamābdika) is indeed performed in that thirteenth month, even though an intercalary month (adhikamāsa) has fallen within it.

Others, however, citing the reading of Yama’s statement, "One should not perform the first annual rite (*ābdika*) at Maṇipura," explain this passage as having the following intent: even if an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) falls in the interim, the first annual rite must be performed in the thirteenth month at Maṇipura. [This applies] when it falls in the interim month.

Regarding the annual śrāddha (*ābdika*) which occurs on whichever month, fortnight, lunar day (*tithi*), or specific day it may touch—by virtue of the prescribed rule—if that [specific] day has been missed, one should perform the second and subsequent annual rites there; however, the first annual rite is not performed then.
Rather, the meaning is that the first annual rite should be performed when the twelfth month has passed and the thirteenth month has arrived, on the very day of its commencement. That—

Because there would be the consequence of numerous faults such as syntactical irregularity (*śranyācāra*), because this statement is not understood from any other passage, and because there is no evidence for assuming an intended meaning by resorting to ellipsis (*abhyāhāra*) and the like;
therefore, of this sentence, only this is [the correct reading]: "One whose first [ancestors] have passed a year, he should perform that [offering] with meat."

The reading seen in the Bālapaṇḍita [tradition] is that the son [is the authority]; therefore, when there is an intercalary month as the thirteenth, the first annual śrāddha (prathamābdika) is performed precisely in that thirteenth month, even though an intercalary month may have occurred in the interval— so says Bihū.
In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, in the section on the determination of time (*kālaniyaya*) within the remaining chapters, Paiṭhīnasi states:
"Noble persons should not perform auspicious rites during an intercalary month."
One who desires his own welfare should not perform what is praised [by others].

[150] Although rites such as those performed for specific desires (*kāmya*) and sacrifices (*iṣṭi*) are prohibited during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*) in general, their commencement and completion are also prohibited during an *adhika-māsa*. However, in the case of a *cayana-māsa*, the prohibition applies only to the initial commencement.

Otherwise, if an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) occurs within the month of Kārttika, there would result the non-completion of the commenced Cāturmāsya vows; and if an intercalary month occurs within the month of Pauṣa, there would follow the necessity of restarting the Māṣa-vrata commenced during the previous fortnight. [End of] the intercalary month.

If that were the case, then the rule for completion in the month of Kārttika and the rule for commencement in the month of Puṣya would be contradicted, whether the completion occurs in the preceding or the following month. Furthermore, it would imply a renewed resolve for commencement in another month for an undertaking already begun that is to be accomplished over many years.

As for the objection [regarding] the commencement, it contradicts the statement of Kātyāyana: "The commencement and completion should take place in the same year. However, in the case of an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), since there is the possibility of joining two different lunar months (*samāsa*), the commencement and completion can logically occur therein; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever in prohibiting those two [actions] during an intercalary month. Regarding the first commencement—
If it is asked, "Why should this [rite] not also take place in an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), since there is no other pure month [available]?"—the answer is:
No, because that would contradict the scriptural injunction: "One should not perform great gifts (*mahādāna*) or solemn observances (*vrata*) in an intercalary month.
This prohibition is intended to forbid the completion and so forth of a rite, provided it has already begun once, except in the case of a *saṅkalpa* (a formal vow or resolution).

For there would be a contradiction regarding the prohibition of commencing optional vows (*kāmyavrata*) and the like in the intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*), as has been stated; however, there is no such contradiction if the prohibition is understood as applying only to the first commencement of optional vows and the like in the intercalary month. Now, this being the case, when the month of Kārttika becomes an intercalary month...

Then, for those who observe the Kārttika vow, since the month of Kārttika begins on the day of Śaṅkha (the second lunar day) and ends on the day of Śukra (the fifth lunar day), even when [the month] arrives thus, the performance of the practice would result in lasting for two months; such is the intention. It is said:
(1) "of Puṣya" [is the reading in manuscript *ya*].
I had the construction of a great palace for my mother completed.

For if the rule for the commencement of the month-long fasting vow (*māsopavāsa-vrata*) were in Āśvina and the rule for its completion in Kārttika, then it would indeed be so; however, this is not the case. Rather, having stated the commencement on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, the completion is prescribed in the *Viṣṇurahasya* as occurring on the subsequent twelfth day of the bright fortnight.
It is beneficial.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina,
one should observe this vow for as many days as there are [in the cycle].
Having thus performed this vow of fasting for a month for exactly thirty days— neither more nor less— the self-restrained practitioner, with senses conquered, [attains the goal].
Then one should indeed worship the Auspicious One, whose banner is Garuḍa, on the twelfth day;
one should honor him with flower garlands, perfumes, flowers, and ointments.
One should feed the best of the twice-born with gifts of land and other offerings,
give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), and conclude the rite after prostrating before them.
Then, having commenced this vow on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, it should be completed on the twelfth day of the subsequent month;

it is not to be performed for two months. This is because the Māsopavāsa vow is optional (kāmya), and for an optional rite, the rule permits its completion even in an intercalary month (malamāsa) provided it was commenced prior to that intercalary month.

The fault of redundancy [is as follows]: Now, when there arises the expectation as to in which month the second annual offering (*dvitīyābdika*) and the *vardhāpana* for those who have died and those who are born should be performed, he states the distinction between the months included within an intercalary month (*cayamāsa*) in order to determine that.
In the first [half], it is the eastern [direction]; in the second, the one to its north;
Māyā and Vidyā are the two wise ones on the left and right, while the two middle ones are Cakrā and Mātrā.
In the first [case], the *tibbai* is the *pūrvīmātha*; in the second, it is the *taduttaro māya*.
Thus, the meaning is that the *māu* in the middle of the *pavamāna* are the *budha* and *khina*. Therefore...
[page 112]
The fourth [type] consists of that which arises from reflection (*cintāmayī*);
regarding the remaining [rites], the annual anniversary (*mṛtābdika*) for one who has died there and the *buddhīpana* [rite] for one born there should be performed in the preceding month.

The distinction is this: for one who has died during the Tiṣya (Puṣya) asterism, the annual anniversary (ābdika) rite should be performed, and the celebration of the birth (vardhāpana) should be performed in the following month.
Thus [ends the work] of the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja, the illustrious Mahādevīyasakatha, the lord of the illustrious Karaṇa.
In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* composed by Śrī Hemādri, who is proficient in all branches of knowledge,
the determination of the months (*māsanirṇaya*) within the determination of time (*kālanirṇaya*) in the section on miscellaneous matters (*pariśeṣa*) is completed.
Now begins the third chapter:
the general determination of all lunar days (*tithi*). A lunar day is of two kinds: complete (*sampūrṇā*) and deficient (*khaṇḍā*). Among these, the complete [lunar day]—the deficient...

It is shown in the Rāṇa: "All [days] beginning with the first lunar day (pratipat), from sunrise until the sun rises again, are renowned as 'complete' (sampūrṇa), excluding the day of Hari (harivāsara). The complete day of Hari will be discussed in the determination of the eleventh day (ekādaśī). An incomplete [day] belongs to two days; such is the rule.

When there arises a doubt as to whether the *pūrvā* (earlier) or *aparā* (later) [tithi] should be adopted for the performance of rites such as the *Mātṛ-pūjā* when it relates to the beginning of a day (*dinādi*), a determination is made. Regarding that, the traditional rule (*nigama*) states:
"In the case of the pairs of Yugas, Agnis, Bhūtas, and the two days of Aśvinī and Vasu... (9).
The twelfth day is deficient, while the fourteenth and the full moon are complete.
Even if one performs [the rites] on the new moon day, the pair of the two [days] is a great conjunction;
it destroys the great fault of these [days] and increases previously accumulated merit.
‘Couple’ (yugma) is the second; ‘Agni’ is the third; ‘Yuga’ is the fourth;
‘Bhūta’ is the fifth; ‘Vaṭ’ is the sixth; ‘Suni’ is the seventh; ‘Vasu’ is the eighth; ‘Randhra’ is the ninth;
‘Dra’ is the eleventh—because it is stated that “the pair” (yugma) refers to the even [numbers], these [names] denote the second and subsequent positions.

The meaning is that, in the sequence of the three [fortnights], in each pair of lunar days (*tithi*), only the pair where the subsequent day is pierced by the previous one yields great fruit; it is not the case that a pair where the preceding day is pierced by the subsequent one does so.
By this, it is stated that in the *Umāyurāmakhaptaka*, the first [lunar day] is pierced by the latter, while the latter is pierced by the former.
(1) *dublāṣi-va-bhūvānām*— thus in Ka0. In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, in the section on the determination of the *bāla* (the ignorant/childish), page 114.

In the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*, regarding the *Dvādaśī* [twelfth day], it is stated: "On even-numbered days, one should offer food to the ancestors; 'even' (*yugmāni*) refers to the fourth case-ending, and 'Rāma' refers to the third case-ending.

Regarding the phrase "and those that have already occurred," some say: "The first day [of the lunar fortnight] is the new moon," because of the statement, "the first day is also the new moon."

The statement of Āpastamba and Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa—"The second lunar day (dvitīyā) shall be joined with the first (pratipad), and the first shall be joined with the second"—refers specifically to the *uṣṇa-pratipad* (the first day of the bright fortnight when it falls on a Sunday). [The lunar days] ending in *ca* are auspicious; specifically, the first day (*pratipad*) joined with the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), because of the statement: "The first day and the new moon.
Likewise, the fifth, the seventh, the tenth, and the thirteenth [lunar days].
And on the new moon day, the lunar date (tithi) must be observed as present when it is in conjunction with the ritual action.
And because of this statement by Paiṭhīnasi:

"In this regard, some explain [the term] *sammukha* as 'extending through the afternoon' (*sāyāhnākrāyin*), based on the statement in the Skanda Purāṇa: 'That which extends through the afternoon is called *sammukha*'. That is incorrect; it will be explained—

Because it would contradict the statement of Mādhava, the passage from the *Skanda Purāṇa* is appropriately understood as referring to another subject. Therefore, in this context, the first lunar day (*pratipad*) joined with the preceding [fortnight] is intended; moreover, that too must extend into the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), according to the *Skanda Purāṇa* statement: "The *pratipad* should be taken when it is joined with the morning (*pūrvasaṃyuktā*) or when it extends into the afternoon. As for the other [passages],...
The second day, whether it be the new moon (*pratipad*) or the full moon (*dvitīyā*), is prescribed for the sacrifice;

however, because of the injunction regarding the *apasavya* (left-hand) ritual, it is not the case that the *pratipad* comes first as the primary element. In that very context, there is this specific rule regarding the sequence of rites: "The rite should be performed on the *pratipad*, or it may be done on the following day."
Generally, the power of the conjunction with the lunar day.

The statement that "the second lunar day should be the one for the commencement" refers exclusively to the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). Furthermore, there is no rule requiring it to be the entire [day];

even the statement of Paiṭhīnasi is said to concern the first day of the bright fortnight (*śuklapratipat*). This being so, the meaning of the injunctions such as "the fifth and the seventh," and "one should perform [the rite] on the first day of the bright fortnight," is merely—
The objection that it would follow [from our position] that the first lunar day (pratipad) is subject to a single injunction— namely, "the pratipad should have a second [day]"—
is equally applicable to both positions; for you resort to abandoning the scope of the Yugmādivākya,
while we resort to abandoning the scope of the Pratipat-sukhāvākya.
Because of its dependence [on a general rule]. Now, one might object: "Is there not a fault in the statement 'the fifth and the seventh'?

For it is logical that a general rule (*sāmānyaśāstra*) be restricted by a specific rule (*viśeṣaśāstra*); otherwise, if it were not so restricted because of the possibility of coexistence, there would result the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all restrictive rules. True, this is so; however, [in this case] the *pratipad* must be performed facing forward (*saṃmukhā*).

Since there is no reason for such a restriction of the statement, it applies to both cases as well. Consequently, even the objection regarding the sentence "the fifth and the seventh [cases] alone" will not apply to our position; nor does the objection regarding the statement "the *pratipad* [vowel] is *sammukha* [before a consonant]" arise, for there is no restriction of this [rule].

Thus it is said. [Objection: But surely, since there would be the complexity of enjoining two distinct meanings—namely, that the first lunar day (pratipad) of the dark fortnight, which has not attained the status of being "pierced by the previous day" (pūrvaviddha), should be pierced by the previous day, and that it should be the latter part of the day—if one were to argue that the first lunar day of the bright fortnight already possesses the status of being pierced by the previous day and thus the injunction applies to that case as well, [we reply: it is said in response:

First of all, the nature of the first lunar day (pratipad) exists as something faultless; therefore, it is prescribed that one should face the first lunar day with a multitude of virtues and perform [the rites] accordingly, so there is no difficulty.
Thus, regarding the first lunar day—

"We have committed an offense in that we gave away a girl whose birth was determined by the *pratipad* tithi being pierced by the previous [tithi], for it is said that a girl so pierced is unfit for marriage. Therefore, it is improper to perform the rite on a *pratipad* that is thus afflicted;
rather, the ritual should be performed on a *pratipad* that is pure, free from such defects, and auspicious. Thus it is prescribed in the injunctions.

However, this fault does not apply when [the word] is intended as the object of the practice of showing respect (*gaurava-pratipatti*). And thus, just as in the sentence "The fifth and the lover," even though the *vaca* (the letter 'va') occurs by force of the rule, it is not a fault; so too here.

Cāṭanī, sandaṇḍī, and trivarātrīya.

As for that which is stated in the *Padmapurāṇa*: "(1) 'The eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) as well as the sixth (*ṣaṣṭhī*)... [Note: *ṣaṣṭhī* appears as *baḍhītī* in the manuscript *kha*.]

The statement, "The [days] following and preceding [the lunar day] should be observed," refers to occasions other than those where the lunar day is joined by the following day (paraviddhā), as established by another scriptural injunction; for a general rule cannot apply to a subject already restricted by a specific rule. By the phrase "all lunar days (*tithayaḥ sarvāḥ*)," there is an exclusion of those [lunar days] other than the *upoṣya-tithi* (the day to be observed as a fast), which is otherwise established by another scriptural injunction as being "pierced by the following day" (*paraviddha*). However, if the word "all" were intended to include even those *upoṣya-tithi*s prescribed by other injunctions as being optionally "pierced by the preceding day" (*pūrvaviddha*) when they are full, then it would serve a purpose.

Therefore, this too is a specific rule (*viśeṣaśāstra*); thus, like the *ekādaśī-tithi*, those [days] other than the *vyaṅga* (defective) ones should be observed optionally as either joined with the preceding day or joined with the following day.
And so, according to the understanding of the *Mādhava-adhikaraṇa*, there is an option between the *bāja* and the *avyaya* (non-declining), as stated by Bhavadeva in the Vārttika.

Let us not [assume] that because there is a conceptual distinction between the general and the particular, there is a contradiction elsewhere; for in all cases, since there is no relationship of sublation between the denotable objects of the general and the particular, those two [categories] are also [not contradictory].
Because it is a specific branch. For instance, if the injunction for the *vana* sacrifice were merely "one should sacrifice with *vaca*," [as on page 167].
In the section concerning the departure for the fast-day observance (upavāsa-tithi-niryāya),
it is heard [in one place], and in another place, there is indeed a distinction consisting of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, as well as the general rule.

This is the principle of the "remainder" (śeṣanyāya); however, although it is stated generally as "all this that is offered in the *udvāsana* [removal] belongs to the sacrifice" (*yajñāya*), the subsequent utterance of the word "all" (*sarva*) in grammatical apposition with that [sacrifice] makes it known that this refers to all the constituent parts (*avayava*) of the primary rite (*prakṛta*) for which no specific substance has been prescribed by the original injunction (*utpattiśiṣṭa*).

It is incorrect to argue that because the word "sacrifice" (yajña) is intended by the injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*) to have only the [specific] subject matter as its scope, there is therefore an option (*vikalpa*) since both [the general and specific rules] have that same specific scope; for if this statement were to apply to guests who are already established by another scriptural injunction, then the prohibition would depend upon the sublation of that other scripture in one instance.

Furthermore, there would result a discrepancy in the injunctions regarding what is "independent" (*nirapekṣa*). Moreover, there would also be a discrepancy in that the injunction would be mandatory (*nityavat*) for guests who have already been fed previously, whereas it would be optional (*vikalpena*) for guests who are fed later.
This is also the case in the passage: "Indeed, whatever clarified butter (*ājya*) is in the *bhuvā* vessel is prepared for the sake of every sacrifice," where the substance is not fixed.

The prescription of *śrī* (rice) in the sacrifice follows from the very reason already stated. Furthermore, if *śrī* were prescribed with reference to the sacrifice, then, for the sake of obtaining a substance not previously mentioned, the qualification "all of it" (*sarvasya*) would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) due to the restatement of a qualified object. Therefore, the word "all" (*sarva*) serves to restate what has already been established. And of that...

The purpose [of the statement] is the praise of what is to be heard (*śrāvya-stuti*), by means of demonstrating its connection with all sacrifices. How then is there an option (*vikalpa*) between *jāghani* and *ājya*? It is said: because of the Taittirīya statement, "The *prayāja*s are performed with *ājya*, and the *patnīsaṃyāja*s with something else," *ājya* is obtained for the *patnīsaṃyāja*s. If it should be argued:

This is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) supplementary to the injunction regarding the *anuvacana* (recitation), and not an injunction for the *ājya* offerings in the *patnīsaṃyāja* rites; for it is heard thus: "A flaw (*jāmi*) is indeed created in the sacrifice when the *prayāja* offerings are made with *ājya* and the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings with *sāmnāyya*;
therefore, one recites the *anuvacana* for the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings and sacrifices with a *ṛc*."

As for the claim that [the word *ājya*] is mentioned merely for the sake of connecting [the substance], that is incorrect; for one must resort to an injunction (*vidhi*) because the statement would otherwise be an unintelligible restatement of what is already established, just as in the case of the rule, "One holds the ladle above the *davi*.

However, the authors of the *Tantravārttika* consider that the substance *ājya* (clarified butter) is obtained from another scriptural passage: "One performs the *patnīsaṃyāja* sacrifices with *ājya*. Therefore...

It is appropriate that this verbal expression [of the word "all"] is subject to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). If it is asked: "Granted that this may be so because the word 'all' has a purposeful application, but how can this be the case here where it is not so?"—it is said in reply:

The word *sarva* (all) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what has not yet been reached, just like the word *ubhaya* (both) in the passage, "If both of one's oblations (*havir*) should meet with ruin. Now, if it were thought that [the term] should be restricted to either the first or the last [offering], then the inclusion of the word *ubhaya* would be for the purpose of removing the misconception that this is like the ruin of a single offering; for even here, the plural number (*bahuvacana*) fulfills its purpose by referring to exactly three.

The mention of the lunar days beginning with the first (pratipad) is for the purpose of dispelling the misconception that [the rule] applies only to the five [specific] days; thus, it will be comprehensive.

Furthermore, since the purpose of dispelling the misconception is accomplished even by other means, it serves no further function; therefore, the same logic applies to both terms, as their purpose is identical. Or rather, what is the use of this inquiry?
The course that applies to both cases regarding gold [as a gift] should be followed here as well, through the application of this very principle.

Furthermore, as for the statement of Gārgya concerning the fast on the Tiṣya day—that "in the bright and dark fortnights, the first [lunar day] is the first and the last is the last"—that too must be understood as referring to a different subject matter, as it contradicts other scriptural injunctions. Now, this is being investigated: when—

When, starting from the day [of the new moon], the subsequent lunar day (*tithi*) increases in duration such that it extends beyond the next sunrise and becomes the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*) or similar, then is it the preceding day that should be observed for fasting (*upoṣyā*), or the following? On this point, some say:
"The following day should be observed for fasting, according to the scriptural injunctions regarding 'pairs' (*yugma*) and so forth."
Whatever vow has been undertaken by one during the day or night on a specific lunar day,
one should perform another vow on the conjunction of the next breath (the following day).

Based on this statement, by abandoning the *thugma* (odd) lunar day, one should perform the vow (*vrata*) on the preceding day itself for the son. Since it is impossible to perform rites such as the birth-observance (*jātakarma*), which are to be accomplished over a full day and night (*ahorātra*) and so forth, when the primary time is unavailable, there arises the possibility of adopting another fixed lunar day proximate to that [primary] time. In this regard, [the rule is given]: "Odd [days] for Agni... and so forth.

By such statements as "of the beings" (*bhūtānām*), specific times for sacrifice are restricted; therefore, it is said that by setting aside the full lunar day (*sampūrṇatithi*), there is the acceptance of even a partial lunar day (*khaṇḍatithi*) due to the force of what is expressed by the word "Bhūta. To this, it is replied:

Regarding the determination of the date for a fast:
whatever portion of the lunar day (tithi) exists on the following day— whether it be a decrease or an increase—
that much of it, even if not seen on the previous day, is to be employed for the ritual.

Thus, by examining the sequence of these scriptural statements, for as many lunar days (*tithi*) as increase on the following day, the preceding lunar day remains in existence until the end of the previous day. Therefore, even by the force of the preceding lunar day, it is proper to perform the rite on the very next day, in order to favor the rule of the *yugma* (pairing) texts.
Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara; there is also another passage:
"The lunar day (tithi) is to be shifted by one [unit]."
Regarding dharma, artha, and kāma, the wise Manu has said:
"Even if it is devoid of fame, that which is abandoned by the great attains growth through its excellence."
Just as the month of Mārgaśīrṣa is the deity of the former [fortnight] and likewise the latter, so too should the former lunar day be abandoned; why then is the latter bound? Thus it is said.

The fast associated with the moon (the *madayukta-upavāsa*) should be performed on the previous lunar day (*pūrvā*), because it must pervade the time of the ritual action; according to the scriptural statement: "On whatever time a rite is to be performed, the lunar day (*tithi*) that pervades that time [is the one to be used]. Furthermore, even if the full moon (*pūrṇā*) is present, it is indeed the same lunar day (*tithi*) [that counts], as stated in the rule regarding the beginning of the lunar day: "At the start of the lunar day..."

As for the statement, "it should be as much as [is required]," meaning that wherever there is *vṛddhi* before a following vowel, to that extent the preceding [element] is [the cause], because it arises after [that point] up until the completion—this too is incorrect; for in that context it was stated, "in the case of an action" (*karmaṇi*), and whatever action is prescribed for a specific lunar day (*tithi*) is its own action; therefore, it is prescribed for the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*).

Likewise, the *supavāsa-vrata* (the fast with excellent observance) is a ritual; therefore, that ritual is not [performed] on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*). Consequently, the mention of the "variegated penance" (*vicitra-prāyaścitta*) refers to the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*), as it is established by the two [scriptural authorities]. Because of the absence of any great purpose for the omission of the fast—given the scriptural statement "one should die by day or night"—it is [restricted to] the even days (*yugmā*).
*Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, Section on the Conquest of Desire, Part 7, Page 170.
By examining the various scriptural statements, it may be that [the vow] occurs even in the absence of the actual form of fasting. Now, if it is argued:

"On account of the statement, 'The wise man should resolve upon the vow of fasting and so forth in the morning,' it must be performed on the morning itself; and thus, even if the lunar day (tithi) suitable for the fast is not obtained on the second day..."

The inclusion of the previous lunar day [as a rule] implies that when both [the previous and current days] cover the entire day and night (*ahorātra*), the rite belongs to the second day alone; however, this too is incorrect, because it would result in the redundancy of the qualification "by day and by night," and because all observances are practiced on the very first day.
"Whichever lunar day (tithi) encompasses the time of the specific desire for a particular rite, one should perform that rite accordingly; the [technical] definition of the tithi is not the cause."

Furthermore, since the two reasons for determining whether a lunar day (*tithi*) belongs to the preceding or following day have been refuted when the *karmakāla* (the time for performing a rite) is being considered, and because the purpose of adopting the "increase" (*vṛddhi*)—which was shown during the discussion on the general determination of all lunar days—is impossible here; [therefore,] "the lunar day... [is not applicable].

The mention of "possessing grain" (*saśasyā*), however, refers to the context of the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*). "Possessing grain" means overlapped by the tenth day (*daśamī-viddhā*); "devoid of number" (*vihīna-saṅkhyā*) means a complete eleventh day (*sampūrṇaikādaśī*). Both of these types are to be rejected. Since the eleventh day increases slightly on the following days, it is said: "Where the eleventh day is complete, it shall be so again at dawn," and so forth.

It should be understood that this [statement] has the same scope as the previous statement. In this way, the contradiction with other statements is avoided, and there will be no need to postulate another underlying *śruti* (Vedic text), whereas if it were to apply to all lunar days (*tithi*), such a postulation would indeed be required. As in the case of the statement, “Just as the *mālīkucā* flower is first,” regarding “all pride” (*sarva-darpa*).
By the statement "the latter two are to be honored," this refers to the same subject matter; however, it does not prevail because it sublates the full lunar day (*sampūrṇatithi*).

Therefore, it is established that in such a case, only the former [lunar day] is to be accepted. But when the latter [lunar day] is to be observed as the fast-day, and there exist even a single *ghaṭikā* on the second day, then those [lunar days] alone are to be observed, and not otherwise.

Alternatively,
when the *nigraha* (suppression) and *ṛtvarāja* (the king of seasons) are joined with the *praśna* (question),

Some have said:

"The word *pāra* signifies the completion of a rite (*karma*), but not the eating; for that [eating] is a duty pertaining to the city (the body), and here the form [of the word] is derived from the verbal root *pāra-tīra*, meaning 'in the completion of an action'."

Regarding the term "pāraṇam" (breaking the fast): likewise, because it consists of giving, fire-offerings, and worship of the deities, and because performing it at night—such as by visiting a king and so forth—is prohibited, it is said that one should fast until the appearance of the stars (*nakṣatra*).
Furthermore, this fasting for the sake of the stars (*nakṣatropoṣaṇa*) is to be understood from the *Nakṣatrapuruṣa* and other such texts, or else from the *Gaya*.

If a fast-day (cheda) cannot be obtained by any means during the day, then it is held that one should perform the worship of the deities and other rites before the meal, and eat only when the [specific] constellation has passed; however, this is incorrect, as it is forbidden on the days of seeing the king, during the solar transits (saṃkrānti), on the days of marriage, and on the days of the full moon and new moon.
Eating, giving, and so forth are prohibited during the Khurṣuṇī festival and during optional vows.
By such statements as these, since acts such as giving are prescribed even at night for optional rites (*kāmya-karma*),

and since practices like the "vow of man" (*puruṣavrata*) are also performed for the sake of specific desires; therefore, [the claim] that "the cutting off of the nose is somehow obtained during the day" and so forth is likewise untenable according to your own position regarding such matters.

Because the moon is liberated from the conjunction with the asterism belonging to the second day; therefore, having determined it thus, if the conjunction with the asterism belonging to the setting [of the sun] occurs on the very first day, then that [day] alone is to be observed; but if the conjunction with the setting does not occur on either of the two days, then likewise [the same applies]; however, when on the previous—
If it belongs to the first day and is connected with the afternoon, or if it belongs to the second day and is connected with the morning, then it is related to the second day;

for there is this scriptural statement: "O limb [of the ritual], whatever time is determined for a rite becomes a constituent part when that rite is commenced, just as the morning is a constituent part when the *gopradāna* is commenced."

There is a statement in the Viṣṇudharmottara:

That refers to a hundred other objects besides the fast.
As for the statement of Baudhāyana:
"The lunar day on which the sun rises while it is still not fully visible..."
But for the waxing fortnight, it proceeds toward setting during its waning.

This refers to the subject matter of the *piṇḍakārya* (the rite of offering the rice-balls). Because the determination of the *macatra* (lunar mansion) is logical, and because the injunction regarding the increase of the lunar day (*tithi*) applies only to the *pillattha* [specific context] and not otherwise, nor does it apply to both cases as being subject to fasting (*upavāsa*), since that is already restricted by specific scriptural rules;
therefore, the systematic arrangement stated by us alone is correct.

In the fourth chapter on the *Cintāmayī* [section] of the *Pārameśvarī*, what is the scope of the plural number? The term *agnihotra* is intended as an illustration for enjoined actions (*vihitakarman*); thus the meaning becomes this: "If a student (*brahmacārī*) does not neglect his life-force (*prāṇa*)—whether through physical harm or through the neglect of enjoined duties—he would incur the fault of being 'defiled' (*avakīrṇin*). And such is the construction: [the offering] to the life-breaths and the *agnihotra*.

"To the Hotṛ priest, likewise with the offering of food"—this is what is meant: even for one such as a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) who performs austerity by means of the *prāṇāgnihotra* and so forth, there is no great fault; however, for a householder (*gṛhastha*) and others, if the *prāṇa*...

Or if the Agnihotra and other such rites were obstructed, then there would be fault; as it is said: "The vital breaths are the cause of the stability of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. What has not been protected by one who protects them? And what has not been protected?"

Thus, because of the two scriptural statements, "Performing actions here indeed, one should desire to live a hundred years," it is established that the functions of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are not to be obstructed. Even though it is said: "That auspicious action by which the body is nourished must be performed to the utmost; that is called non-negligence (*anālasya*)."

Thus, this [prohibition] is intended to prevent extreme suffering and not merely to avoid suffering altogether; therefore, it is established that those living as householders have the right to perform fasts and other such observances. "Only those who are infinite proceed [to the goal]; for those who are not infinite, there is no attainment"—thus it is said regarding death. It is replied:
Does this statement enjoin eating for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), or does it prohibit fasting?
Even if eating is enjoined, is it being stated that it must be done at all times?

Or rather, when there is a desire to eat, provided that no obstacle exists and food is available, one should eat; for even though other scriptures do not authorize eating before [the prescribed time], this rule is established as a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to eating. The injunction "one who is impure shall eat" is thus rendered applicable. Nor should it be said that one must eat even when there is an obstacle [to the usual rules], for that is impossible. Furthermore, eating is not being re-permitted in places, times, or conditions not authorized by other scriptures; for if that were the case, then even at times such as those involving eclipses (sagraha), etc., [eating would be required].

It would follow that even in a place such as Māśāna, food that has stood overnight or is otherwise unfit would have to be eaten by one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), even though he is fasting. If you say, "Let it be so," then alas, what a painful thing this is heard!
Oh, how great is their greed for food, since they act contrary to the well-known consensus of all respectable people even regarding auspicious occasions (*maṅgalādi*)!

"Eating" is what is being discussed; furthermore, many scriptures contradict this by prohibiting specific objects, such as the injunctions "one should not eat during an eclipse of the moon or sun," and so forth. Now, one might object that because those are general rules (*sāmānya-śāstra*), they must refer to those who have not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*). To this it is replied: either this [present rule] refers to objects other than those already prohibited, or—

It is not so stated; for just as prohibitory scriptures are called "general" (*sāmānya*) because they apply equally to those who have maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and those who have not, so too the scripture concerning food is a "general" scripture because it applies equally to both prohibited and non-prohibited objects. If this is the case, then there must be an option (*vikalpa*) [between eating and not eating], if you say that. To that we reply: no.

Because the injunctions are inconsistent. Likewise, in the case of statements such as "Only those who possess infinite [merit] succeed" and "One should not eat during an eclipse of the moon or sun," since these are presented as descriptions of existing facts (*vartamānāpadeśa*), they do not constitute an injunction (*vidhi*). Therefore, there is no optionality (*vikalpa*) here. But is it not the case that this involves excessive effort, given that eating is already established for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) through the *saṅgraha* and other rites?

It is asked: "What must be observed on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) and so forth? It is replied: What partiality is there in this? For just as the scriptural prohibition "one should not eat during an eclipse of the moon or sun" is explicit, so too does the scripture exist stating, "one should not eat at night. Therefore, there is a contradiction with another scripture.

This is the rule for the destruction [of the senses] when the object is obstructed by passion. As for the claim that "they succeed only in the infinite," the status of [the Veda] as an injunction regarding objects has already been refuted; therefore, no destruction whatsoever is enjoined here by this [text].

In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, in the section on the *Pariśeṣakāṇḍa*, it is stated that the twice-born must perform the fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*) in the evening and the morning, as enjoined by the Vedas.
One should not eat in between [the prescribed times], for this is the rule comparable to the Agnihotra sacrifice.

This is the injunction regarding eating; however, as before, one might object that it is possible to refute this by asking: "What is the injunction regarding eating at that [specific] time? Since eating is already established through natural desire (*rāga*), the prohibition is made with respect to a specific portion of that meal—namely, eating at the morning time—while everything else is restated (*anūdyate*). Thus, even in this case, it does not constitute an independent injunction.
It is possible [to interpret the injunction] as a prescription for eating qualified by time, because an injunction for two separate times would result in a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).

Therefore, the intended meaning here is simply that eating occurs only in the evening and the morning, and not in between; this is established as a necessary conclusion. Thus, the equality [of the two times] is understood, and when the verbal root-meaning is restated, these [injunctions] are merely secondary (*anyapara*) in their purpose.
Injunctions are accepted such as "one should eat facing the east," and so forth.

Now, one might ask: how can there be a mandatory requirement for morning and evening [meals] for one established in the vows of initiation (*dīkṣita-vrata*)? By the previous statement itself, "one should know," since there is already a prohibition against the connection of the vow with midday or midnight, this further negation of the absence of the vow would be redundant; it certainly makes one understand that [the vow] must indeed be observed.
