Since there is an injunction stating that "only what is fit to be eaten (kicamācam) is to be consumed," the eating of the remainder is also necessarily required because it is prompted by the substance to be disposed of, even in the absence of desire or other such motives; for the statement "in the evening and morning for the twice-born" does not merely enjoin a prohibition against other times, and thus the same applies to the statement regarding those who have maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni).

Let it be that the commencement of the body [of the rite] occurs before sunrise on the new moon day; however, one must state that it will be performed when five *ghaṭikās* have elapsed, because the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), which impels the person toward the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) consisting of both primary and subsidiary elements simultaneously, prohibits any delay in the interim. Therefore, there is no alternative to these two statements.

Even when the morning time (*prātaḥkāla*) is understood as consisting of three *muhūrtas* or as consisting of one and a half *praharas*, according to the injunction of Āpastamba, it must be accepted as consisting of exactly three *muhūrtas*; therefore, for the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice at this time, this very division must be adopted. [Objection: But [it is] twofold—

In a case where the junction (sandhi) occurs for only a mere *ghaṭikā* after the turning point (*āvartanā*) during the division [of the day], the sacrifice (*yāga*) must indeed take place on the following day; yet even there, because of the impossibility of the time, there is a contradiction with that very scriptural statement. It is not so; for since the time—such as "the fourth part of the *parvan*" and so forth—is understood to be connected to the sacrifice, this [junction] must pertain to the sacrifice.

It must be accepted that [the sacrifice] follows the time [of the conjunction]. Since the sacrifice is performed on the following day when the conjunction occurs on the previous day, there is no contradiction in the fact that the sacrifice takes place on the previous day itself. But if this were so, would it not contradict the injunction for the sacrifice on the following day when the conjunction occurs in the afternoon? Not so; for [the rule applies] when the conjunction occurs in the afternoon on the following day.
On the fourth day of the lunar fortnight, there is no *bāga* (division/portion); likewise, in that same state, there is no *aparātalāca-pakṣa*.

And there is no contradiction in [the statement] "the section on determination (*nirṇayaprakaraṇa*) is connected to the preceding," for it is intended for the person; otherwise, it would apply at every moment during the winter season.

If the turning point (*āvarttana*) occurs when the time is slightly less than fourteen *nāḍikās*, then, due to the increase of that very lunar day (*tithi*), sometimes even a fourth part consisting of one *nāḍikā* remains; in that case, the sacrifice (*yāga*) would necessarily be commenced on the following day itself, joined with the interval of just one *ghaṭikā* after the turning point. And not on that [same] day.

Because it occurs at a specific time, because of the prohibition "one should not sacrifice," and because it is possible on the previous day, the term *aparāhṇa* (afternoon) used in conjunction with the word *śruta* (heard/scriptural) is indeed more appropriate; for the statement, "The deity is to be praised until the seventh muhūrta," refers to a period distinct from the prescription of the morning time (*prātaḥkāla*).

This must also be accepted by you; otherwise, since the day is divided into three parts, there would be the undesirable consequence of the sacrifice being performed even when [the sun] has passed into the third part, such as the morning (*prātarādi*). Therefore, the two parts—the preceding and the following—of the location divided into two are indeed what are designated as *pūrvāhṇa* (forenoon) and *aparāhṇa* (afternoon).

In that regard, when the junction of the lunar phases (*parvasandhi*) occurs during the afternoon, the sacrifice is to be performed on the following day; when it occurs during the forenoon, the sacrifice is to be performed on that very day. However, the mention of "midday" (*madhyāhna*) is for the purpose of establishing that when the junction of the lunar phases occurs at the junction between the forenoon and the afternoon, the sacrifice is indeed on that same day. For the term "midday" is technical (*pāribhāṣika*).
Having set aside the midday [offering], he establishes only the middle *caṇa*. For this very reason, Prātātapa also recites the word "middle" (*madhyama*) alone.
If the parvan concludes either during the first or the middle watch of the day,
then the fast is observed on the preceding day; that is declared for its sake.

Regarding the fourfold division [of the day], it is stated in the *Gobhila-smṛti*: "The first [watch] proceeds together with the morning; then midday, and likewise the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*); thereafter the evening (*sāyāhna*). Furthermore, [the *Vasiṣṭha-smṛti* states]:
"The morning (*prātaḥ*) lasts for three *muhūrtas*; the *saṅgava* period is of the same duration; midday (*madhyāhna*) is from [the end of the third *muhūrta*] until the sun has passed the meridian."

"Rātri (the night) is also like that; the three *muhūrtas* at the end of the day (*sāyāhna*) are excluded from all religious duties. According to this statement by Vyāsa, the fivefold division [of the day] is to be understood in the same manner as the sixfold division for other ritual acts.
In the fourth chapter, consisting of reflection,
concerning the determination of the object: the division of the threefold nature of the supported is [discussed] even by those who possess the fortune of the Vajra-like [samādhi].
According to those who follow the *Nibandhas*, it is indeed as stated by Laugākṣi:

"The sacrifice should take place on the very next day at the junction of the night, because of the statement of Laugākṣi, 'In the afternoon or at night,' and because of the statement of Gobhila, 'The ends of the fortnights (pakṣāntas) are to be observed for fasting; the beginnings of the fortnights (pakṣādayas) are to be sacrificed upon. Now, [one might object]: "Is it not the case that after sunset, the *parvan*..."

If the New Moon (*amāvāsyā*) is completed at the junction (*sandhi*) on the fourteenth day, either before or after sunset, and there is a connection with the entire night, then the milking and other rites should be performed at that very time; for it is stated in the Śruti: "Because they bring together (*amāvayanti*) this night here, therefore it is called *amāvāsyā*; having caused the cows to low toward it, he brought them together."
Because the collection of Soma—in the form of curds and other ingredients—by the gods occurs on the new moon day joined with the night;

nor is there a contradiction with the statement, "The *paśu* and others are to be pressed [at dawn]," for that is possible even when [the new moon] extends across both day and night; nor is there a contradiction with the statement, "In the afternoon or at night."

Because it is possible for that [rite] to occur on the full moon as well, and because it would be difficult to maintain [the rule] otherwise, it is said: since the word *rātri* (night) is used figuratively (*upacāra*) to denote the lunar day (*tithi*), and because we see the word *ahar* (day) used in the same sense in such passages as, "If he should not perceive [it] on that very day from the front,
he should fast on that [following] day," and "He does not eat on that night from the front."
Because there is also seen in some places the reading of the word *paścāt* [in the sense of "afterwards"],
as in: "And when he was not seen from the front nor from behind on that night," where the non-perception from the front occurs at the end of the preceding night,
and the non-perception from behind occurs at the beginning of the subsequent night, or alternatively, the non-perception from both the front and the back occurs within that very same night.
This must be explained. In the first case, there would be the very same non-perception as during the day.

In the second case, since that same form exists even in the subsequent night, it would likewise be so [i.e., there would be non-perception]. If it were argued that because one perceives the moon existing on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad) during the subsequent night, perception occurs on the pratipad as well.
And the Karmopādhyāya said:
"The vision occurs on the very day one undertakes it.
Kātyāyana, however, said that it occurs on the new moon day of the month of Āśvayuja.
The section on the determination of the time for the conjunction of the new moon: In the eighth part of the fourteenth lunar day, the moon becomes hot.
"And then, at the eighth part of the new moon (amāvāsyā), it indeed becomes minute.
This [view] is incorrect; for if that which is prohibited by scripture even due to its connection with the night were established, then—

Since the commencement of the first lunar day (pratipad) has already begun, one might think that the fast should not be observed on the previous day because the fourteenth day (caturdaśī) exists [only] at night;
nevertheless, because the moon is still present, the fast must indeed be observed. Thus it is stated in the Smṛti:
If twice-born men perform a funeral feast or a rite for the ancestors on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, which is the day of the spirits,
all of that shall become fruitless.

‘Vihāra’ means wandering, in the sense of moving about for the sake of grazing and so forth; in that context, the elision of the suffix *tal* would be expected. Therefore, it is more logical that the days ending with the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) should be observed as fasting days (*upavasatha*), and the days beginning with the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) should be entered upon for sacrifice. Thus, when there is an intention [to perform the sacrifice] on the night, the sacrifice takes place on the following day. Now, [one might object]: "But on the night..."

Even regarding the *yoginī*, why is the sacrifice (*yāga*) performed on the fifth lunar day (*pañcamī*) when it falls on the first day (*pratipad*), given the statement: "If the second day is marked by the junction" (*ciharttā dvitīyā cet*)? It is because of the understanding of a specific distinction. Furthermore, although the scripture concerning the junction of night (*rātrisandhi*) applies to the entire day...

On the first lunar day (*pratipad*), there is scope for the rule [concerning the *prathamā*]; on the second lunar day (*dvitīyā*) and so forth, there is scope for the rule [concerning the *dvitīyā*] during the daytime conjunction (*divā-sandhi*).

And although the statement "the *pañcamī* and others are to be understood" is based merely on a comparison with usage—thereby avoiding the fault of being sublated by this [present] rule—even so, because the rule regarding the nighttime conjunction (*rātri-sandhi*) cannot be established otherwise, [the rule applies]: "the *pañcamī* and others..."

For this very reason, since the [sacrificial] thread (*dhāga*) falls on the following day in many cases, and because there is no attainment of the fourth part of the *parvan* on the preceding morning, one cannot expect to cause [the sacrifice] to be attained on the previous day until the time of the *muhūrta* [of the *parvan*]. Therefore, having observed the eclipse at the junction of night, one should consider another subject entirely.

The husband; we shall explain that further on. Therefore, it is established that in the case of a nocturnal union, the sacrifice occurs on the following day; and likewise, even in the case of a union occurring after midday, the sacrifice takes place on the following day.
In the *Cintāmayī Bhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, within the section on the determination of time (*kālanirṇaya*) in the *Pariśeṣa-vastu*:
Now, [it may be argued]:

"If on the fourteenth day the fourth part of the lunar day is not seen, and the first day of the new moon (*pratipad*) occurs on the following morning, then the rites for the ancestors (*kavya*) and so forth should be performed on that [fourteenth] day."
Because of this statement, one does not perform the ritual action on the previous day; likewise, there is another scriptural passage:
"If the four-watch period of the fourteenth day [of the dark fortnight] is not obtained during the new moon."
"When the next day has dawned, it should be the first lunar day (pratipad); one should cause it to be performed at the very beginning of that [day]. Thus [it is said].

Even if on the fourteenth day the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) does not extend across all four watches (*yāma*) but only across a portion of them, nevertheless, if the first lunar day (*pratipad*) occurs on the following day, the meaning is that the fast (*upavāsa*) must be observed on the preceding day itself. This is because of the statement of Kātyāyana: "When there is an increase [of the moon] later, one should proceed with the new moon [rite]," where...
On the day of arrival (*pratipad*), there is the occurrence of the *cāturhotṛ-havir-iṣṭi* as a penance (*prāyaścitta*).
It is said: its occurrence on the first day (*pratipad*) is established even when the second day (*dvitīyā*) exists; otherwise, it would be [logically] untenable.
Furthermore, Baudhāyana has stated the word "subsequent" (*parāñcaḥ*); therefore, the sacrifice (*āgama*) takes place on the second day. But when...?

If the fourth part of the lunar day (*parvan*) does not exist on the morning of the preceding day, but exists on the morning of the following day, then on which day should the *sthāpanā* rite be performed? It cannot be on the preceding day, because at that time there is no presence of the fourth part of the lunar day or similar requirements, and thus the time for the *sthāpanā* is absent; furthermore, the junction of the lunar days (*parvasandhi*) occurs later.

Nor can the sacrifice be performed on the following day, because even then the prescribed time is absent. Regarding this, some say: "The sacrifice must be performed on the following day, because the prescribed time—consisting of the fourth part of the *parvan* and so forth—is impossible on the preceding day, and because there is no factor that would cause the sacrifice to be postponed until the fourth part of the first lunar day (*pratipad*). This is the view.
That which exists is a negation that turns one back;
one must not eat in the fourth part of the day, nor at the time of the *pratipad* [new moon] when there is no fire.
"Rākṣasas prowl there"—this is the eternal Vedic revelation.
It is said: this negation concerns the juncture of the middle path, not the juncture of the other extreme.
The section on the completion of the preceding day's ritual portions:

because the sacrifice is prescribed for the following day. However, since the sacrifice on the following day would already be established by the mere conjunction with the afternoon (aparāhṇa), and because the prohibition presupposes such an established possibility, it is appropriate that the prohibition applies precisely there where the fourth part of the *pratipad* occurs.

However, since the performance of the sacrifice is prescribed on the previous day during the middle *sandhi*, there is not even a scent of the fourth part of the *pratipad* [lunar day]; thus, the prohibition [of performing it when the moon rises in the fourth part] would be untenable. To this it is replied: "The phrase 'the *pratipad* and so forth should be sacrificed upon' applies whether the lunar day is complete or a partial lunar day; in that case, on the second day, [if the moon rises] in the fourth part of the *pratipad*..."

Since it occurs at the time of dawn, the fact that the prohibition is preceded by a prior attainment (or possibility) is indeed established. However, this does not imply that one incurs sin by performing the sacrifice on the fourth day of the dark fortnight (*pratipad-caturthī*). For it is prescribed there that "the *Pañcādi* sacrifices are to be performed"; since the sacrifice is thus enjoined, when there is both an injunction and a prohibition, there can only be an option (*vikalpa*).
And in the *Tīrthadārtika*:
"Even if one has obtained some object within the scope of a ritual injunction,
if one should entertain the thought that it is a transgression, that [act] rests upon an alternative option (*vikalpa*)."
For in perception, injunctions and prohibitions have the same force and the same object;
therefore, one of them must be followed by those who regard it as authoritative.
This fault does not apply to those who prohibit [the consumption of] ears of grain while they themselves do not perform it;
however, in that case, the injunction would lack the authority characterized by being a Vedic command.
But if the injunction is accepted as authoritative, since the negation is sublated by it,
the definition of Dharma as "that which is characterized by Vedic injunction" remains free from defect.
And it must be stated that an option (vikalpa) is not appropriate because, although the rule "the *pac*-class [roots] are to be treated as *abhiṣṭu* [etc.

has scope as a general provision even when there is a conflict with the fourth case, the rule "the *na-ya-ha-vyaṃ* [roots] are in the fourth part" is without scope due to its specific restriction to the third and fourth cases; for [the latter] is a specific [rule].
Even in the case of a prescription regarding an object, there is no absolute sublation by a specific prohibition, because [the general rule] is dependent upon that [specific one].
In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*,
in the section on the *Pārvaṇa* rites, it is stated by the author of the *Vārttika* in his commentary:

Even though the injunction (*vidhi*) is weak, it becomes strong through a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) that derives its very existence from it; this will be explained under the sections on "prohibition" (*pratiṣedha*), "injunction based on a specific context" (*pradeśa*), and "injunction of what has not been previously established" (*ārabhyavidhāna*).
Therefore, since an absolute prohibition of a matter already established by scripture is impossible, [the rule applies] to those [who are not *anuyājans*].

The option (*vikalpa*) is like [the case of] "one performs the *yajāmahe*," and not exactly like that; for in that case, the option can be avoided by resorting to an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). To explain: since the time directly enjoined—consisting of the three parts beginning with the fourth quarter of the *parvan*, the fourth day, and the first day—is non-existent on both days at the morning time, [an option would otherwise arise].

Since the sacrifice cannot be omitted because it is not enjoined as something optional, and because it is impossible to abandon a rite that has been prescribed, it follows—by virtue of the consistency of the injunction regarding performance—that the sacrifice must be performed even if there is some deficiency in the time. Thus, on the previous day at the morning time, even though the fourth part of the *parvan* (the junction period) is absent, the sacrifice should be performed because the *parvan* itself still exists; or else, [it should be performed] on the following day during the *pratipad*.

Even in the absence of the division of inheritance (*dāyabhāga*), since the existence of the *pratipad* (the first lunar day) remains, the performance [of the rite] must take place; thus, even when the *pratipad* falls on the fourth part of the day, the occasional (*naimittika*) attainment cannot be prevented by either of the two views. Therefore, since an option (*vikalpa*) is unavoidable when establishing an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it is better to accept the option for the sake of maintaining the primary sense (*mukhyārtha*).

Furthermore, the particle *na* must indeed be expressive of a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). Moreover, it is a prohibition because an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is impossible. To explain: first, because there is no distinction [in the case of the new moon] regarding its being devoid of the fourth part of the first lunar day (*pratipad*). If, on the other hand, [the view were that] one should sacrifice on a *pratipad* that is devoid of the fourth part, then—

In the fourth part of the *parvan*, the time for sacrifice (*bāga*) is not attained. Now, if it is argued that one should sacrifice at the time enjoined when the first day (*pratipad*) has increased by four [muhūrtas], then even in the case where the subsequent day is enjoined at the junction of the *parvan*, only the fourth part of the *pratipad* remains; therefore, as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*), how could it be prescribed elsewhere?

[Objection: "One should not look at the rising sun"—here, because of the connection with the word *na* (not), a resolve (*saṃkalpa*) to avoid looking is enjoined. [Response: It is rightly said that in that case, since looking is already established by worldly custom, its prohibition is stated. But here, since the act of speaking on the following day is obtained through the scripture (*śāstra*), it is not [the case that it is merely a restatement].
The section on the method for the removal of obstacles through the *dhūmavandha* (smoke-binding) rite.

The *paryudāsa* (exclusion) can be established here. Nor can it be maintained that, as in the case of the *ārṣeya-varaṇa* (selection of ancestral priests) obtained through the *codaka* (general rule), an exclusion is not possible because of the superior force of the direct instruction "he does not select an *ārṣeya*," so it cannot be found here either.

For both [types of exclusion]—the exclusion that results in the attainment of a fourth part of the practice—are taught in the scriptural branches. Nor is it possible that, just as there is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the *ye yajāmahe* formula—which is applicable to sacrifice in general—from specific sacrifices such as the *anuyāja*s, so too would it be here; for the scriptural rule of exclusion does not [apply] to the divisions of time such as the forenoon or afternoon.
In this regard, it is possible for a specific rule (*viśeṣa-śāstra*) to apply with respect to a general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) concerning the junctions of the *parvan* such as the *aparāhṇa*.

Nor can the exclusionary rule (*paryudāsa-śāstra*) be considered stronger on the grounds of being a direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), because its status as a *śruti* is not established. For instance, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), having stated that the prohibition of the fourth [part] is based on the word of Kātyāyana, said: "One must not [eat] the fourth..."

The verse beginning with "ceṃ'śai" has been recited. Therefore, with the intention of establishing its basis in Śruti, it is said: "This is the eternal Śruti. Now, an objection is raised: since the suffix -tavya is heard in the prohibitive statement (*paryudāsa*), the injunction is explicit; whereas in the statement regarding the junctions (*parvasandhi*) of the *aparāñca* and other [times], because it is expressed as a description of the present (*vartamānāpadeśa*), how can it be considered an injunction? To this, [the author] says:

There is indeed a disparity regarding attainment; this is not so. In the case of a *paryudāsa* (exclusion), there is a doubt as to whether it is a quarter, a half, or a third, which is removed by whatever delay [is required];

likewise, in the other case [the *prasajya-pratiṣedha*], the doubt as to whether it is a present-tense designation or a fifth [element]—expressed by the particle *ca*—is also removed. In the *paryudāsa*, its purpose is to serve as a qualification (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Thus there is an additional fault. Therefore, since an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is impossible, a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) is inevitable. This being the case regarding the option, the scope of the prohibition is the junction between midday and afternoon, while the scope of the injunction is the junction between the forenoon and afternoon. For this reason, by the *Saṃgraha*, [the rite] is performed in the forenoon—due to the distinction between the scopes of the junctions of the forenoon and the afternoon.

The rule for the application of the conjunction (*yoga*) on the first day (*pratipad*) and subsequent days has been established by the statement beginning with “in the forenoon or at midday,” and so forth.
As for the statement, “the fourth part of the two junctions (*parvan*) [is forbidden],” that too does not exclude the performance of the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) during the fourth part of the *pratipad*.
For it does not prohibit the fourth part of the [lunar] day itself, as it is not specifically restricted.

Because it is not perceived as having the nature of a prohibition; nor does it exclude another meaning from the mantra by being an injunction for other preceding parts, since it is not perceived as an injunction due to the absence of injunctive suffixes.
118. In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, in the section on supplements (*pariśeṣakhaṇḍa*), in the determination of time (*kālaniyaya*).
Nor can an injunction be assumed here on the grounds that it is a restatement of an established fact— like the statement "he holds [the vessel] above the gods"—

since there is no contradiction with other means of knowledge. However, in this case, regarding the rule "on the fourth part of the *parvan*," if one were to assume an injunction for the three parts of the *pratipad* with the purpose of excluding the fourth part, [it would be untenable].

The scriptural injunction permitting the cooking of the fourth portion—namely, that "one should not sacrifice the fourth portion"—is contradicted [if it were otherwise]. Nor should it be argued that the suffix is a gerundive (*vijñeya*), since it is equally applicable as having the sense of a gerundive (*kṛtya*). Or, even if it were a prescriptive suffix, nevertheless...

"But since it is already known through cognition (*jñāna*), why perform the sacrifice? Now, [the opponent argues: "Just as in the case of the *nirvāpa* (offering) and the *ālambha* (seizing), even a rule that pertains to a substance not yet cognized effects the desired purpose.
To this it is replied: That too involves a strained interpretation; thus, it lacks the capacity to subvert the clearly manifest scriptural injunction regarding the fourth part. For instance:

The meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is enjoined by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). In the absence of that, either another [element] is enjoined in relation to the meaning of the verbal root, or something else is enjoined within the meaning of the verbal root itself.

However, where something entirely different is enjoined [in relation to] something else, that is excessively strained. Now, if—in order to avoid that fault—the knowledge itself is enjoined in relation to the meaning of the verbal root, how then [is this applied] to time?

[This is] attainment (*prāpti*). Now, it is said that knowledge (*jñāna*), being enjoined, consists in the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the object of knowledge; and since this is untenable without an application (*viniyoga*) of that which is to be refined by the knowledge within the *kāmadhātu*, it necessitates the postulation of an injunction of application (*viniyogavidhi*). In that case, the postulation of the application of the object to be refined arises from the untenability of the refinement itself.

Because it has been refuted in the *Makkādhikaraṇa*. Now, one might object: "Just as the application of the *phalacamasa* and the *pūtīka* plants to the sacrifice was inferred—on the grounds that the consecrations of eating and pressing would otherwise be inexplicable—through the injunctions 'In the absence of soma, press the *pūtīkas*' and 'One should offer him [the *phalacamasa*] as a source of fear'..."
[Objection: Why is a rule for the application (*viniyoga*) of time—which is to be refined by knowledge—not postulated here as well?

[Response: It is said: it is appropriate because Soma, whose application is already established by the injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma," has its consumption and extraction determined by the name (*samākhyā*) "he presses Soma" and "the Soma-cup."
Since it is established that the procedure for preparation does not contradict [the primary injunction], the eating and the pressing are indeed preparations of the Soma.

In the case of a substance whose refinement (*saṃskāra*) has already been established, it is easy to assume that the substance performs the same function as the previous substance by means of the injunction for a refinement involving another substance; however, here, since the refinement of knowledge (*jñāna-saṃskāra*) is not firmly established,
it cannot be sustained unless there is an application (*viniyoga*) obtained through another means of proof (*māna*), as in the case of the *makha-adhikaraṇa*.
This is indeed appropriate.
Furthermore, when the substance of Soma itself, having been assigned [for a rite], is at some time unavailable, its substitute—

When the mental visualization (*dhyāna*) has already been established as a requirement, the rule "one should press the *pūtīka* plants" is merely a restriction (*niyama*), and not an original application (*apūrva-viniyoga*). However, in this case, it cannot be accomplished without another means of application; therefore, [the text says] "one visualizes the ocean with the mind, and the earth with the mind."

The goddesses meditate with their minds; since it is said "meditating," the time-injunction serves merely as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*), and thus there is no prescriptive force regarding the time. Or rather, let it be so: because knowledge is established by its object when the causal complex for knowledge is present, it cannot be an object of injunction; therefore, it is indeed a time-injunction, and the time is not [independently] enjoined.

Regarding the phrase "of him" (*masya*): even so, it is entirely untenable that within a single word such as *yāgakāle* (at the time of sacrifice), something is suggested while something else is expressed, just as in the case of *yajateḥ liṭ-lakāraḥ* (the *liṭ* suffix of the root *yaj*) or *aṣaṅkartuḥ prathamabhakṣaḥ* (the first portion for the one who does not eat). For just as [in those cases], this is qualified by the *vaṣaṭ*.

In that case, it is not possible to enjoin the relationship of primacy; rather, the meaning of the word "time" (kāla), which is qualified by other words such as "the third part" or "the fourth part," and which is subsequently presented as a constituent of the compound term "sacrifice-time" (yāgakāla),
is enjoined later in relation to the meaning of another constituent part of that compound.
It is not tenable [to claim] that there is a connection with another word prior to the mutual connection of the words being compounded, according to the maxim: "A complete word requires another word.

First, after experiencing a connection with the action, there is a mutual connection between the words;

Alternatively, in order to avoid the fault of *vākyabheda*, if one disregards the qualifications such as "fourth part" and so on, and [enjoins] the sacrifice of the *parvan* alone—

Question: Why is a distinction not made regarding the nature of cognition? Answer:

It is said that cognition, if untouched by an injunction (*vidhi*), is not established as valid. Now, if it is touched by an injunction, then that very [cognition] results in the enjoining of multiple things. Objection: Even when touched by an injunction, it does not touch [multiple things] by implication (*arthāt*).

It is not a fault that there is an injunction of multiple parts by means of the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) in that case. Do not say so. For it is not the case that the injunction of the parts would be untenable without this specific excellence (*viśeṣa*), such that one would imply this very specific excellence through the force of the meaning (*artha*). Indeed, the mere mention of what is common does not, simply by being expressed, result in the cognition of a specific excellence; for if that were so...

In every case, there is the sublation of the injunction of a quality. Having enjoined the substrate through the scriptural statement "one should sacrifice with Soma," once the injunction has reached its conclusion, the general expectancy for a substance—which remains in the intellect even without a further injunction—is satisfied by that specific substance, Soma; how then could there be an injunction of a specific [quality]?

Even in a case where, upon the application [of a rule], a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) would result from the injunction of multiple qualities, one may still maintain that only a single quality is being enjoined; for it can be argued that the other specific quality is implied by the impossibility of the general [injunction] otherwise being fulfilled.

If it is argued that in that case, by the statement, "On the day following the *parvan*, the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) should be performed by the twice-born," how can the fourth part of the *parvan* be enjoined for the sacrifice? For even there, the aforementioned defects remain equally applicable. It is replied: [The phrase is] "on the day following the *parvan*."
The two objects in the form of the nooses, characterized by their mutual relationship and unified as one, are enjoined for the sacrifice;

thus, because there is no difference in the thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*), there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). 1] The Section on the Determination of the Time of the Parvan Junctions.
The final quarter of the fifteenth day and the first three quarters of the first [lunar day] constitute the time for the Pārvaṇa sacrifice; otherwise, it is not found.

Thus, the connection between "fifteenfold" (*pañcadaśyāḥ*) and "foot" (*pādaḥ*) is enjoined. Now, an objection: if this were so, the sacrifice would also apply to the first foot of the fifteenfold [stoma], since it is specified as "the subsequent foot. If that is the case, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). This is not a fault, because [the text says] "one should sacrifice at the junction" (*sandhau yajeta*). Thus, regarding the junction—

Since the time prescribed for the sacrifice is unfit [for the specific action], and a time proximate to the junction (*saṃdhi*) must be indicated, when the question arises as to whether it is a *nāḍikā*, a *prahara*, or a *tithi*— given that the proximity of the action is desired— the fifteenth part [of the day] fulfills the requirement for a specific degree of proximity.

That which is prescribed for the purpose of filling [the deficiency] exists as something even closer to the junction (sandhi) by virtue of its proximity, not as something distant. Now, one might object: "In this sentence, is it not the case that we perceive not only the connection between the *pañcadaśī* and the *upāṃśu*, but also another connection with the sacrifice? This is indeed true; however, [it is said] "on both sides of the *parvan*..."

However, since the *iṣṭi* (sacrifice) is enjoined as something to be performed, it is restated (*anūdyate*) because a restatement is possible even for that which is yet to be obtained. Therefore, in the sentence concerning the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*), the purpose of taking the fifteenth day is enjoined.
The mere connection of that [day] with the sacrifice is enjoined by the statement, "on the third part of the parvan."

The fact that the *turīyāṃśatva* (the state of being a fourth part) of that *parvan* is not prescribed [by another rule] but is rather restated (*anūdyate*) from the rules concerning the *sandhi* has already been explained previously by the statement: "A fourth part of the *parvan*. By this, only the connection with the morning *kāsa* is prescribed, while everything else is restated. Therefore, since there is no prescription of multiple meanings in any single instance, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

[This would result in] a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Now, it might be argued that since the connection of the fifteen-fold [stoma] with the foot is established by another sentence, it does not cause a syntactical split when that sentence is intent upon enjoining the connection with the sacrifice.
If that is so, then by the sentence "on the two parvan days, on the fourth," the connection of the sacrifice with the fifteen-fold [stoma] could also be enjoined.

It is indeed possible; it is truly possible. However, that specific time must be prescribed for the *vāgā* (offering), and that [time] is not established even by the prescription of the desire (*kāma*) which consists of the morning in its general form.
In the determination of time regarding the remaining [sections] consisting of four parts produced by reflection,
it is not logical [to claim] that the qualified [meaning] arises from a different sentence, because it is established by another sentence.

Even when the injunction is divided into separate sentences, some degree of complexity is unavoidable in comparison to the injunction of the mere essential form (*svarūpa-mātra*), because it requires dependence on other sentences that establish the qualified [object]. However, where there is no suitable means for the injunction of the mere essential form, there is no alternative recourse.
Even that which has been enjoined for the sake of a sacrifice is indeed prescribed [again], as in the case of "parvaṇo 'turīye" (in the fourth part of the parvan).
Now, if the qualification of both time and portion is effected by one sentence,
and the connection of that qualified [entity] with the sacrifice is effected by another sentence, then by this very method, each [element] is established.

Others do not accept this view of the three divisions beginning with the *acchanna*. Why? And thus, this being the case, there will be a common scriptural basis for the two statements— "The *pratipad* and [subsequent days] are to be sacrificed upon"— and "One should not sacrifice on the fourth part"— by means of their sharing the same three-part division of the *pratipad*.
As for the objection raised against the position of *paryudāsa* (exclusion) regarding the six *ghaṭikās* consisting of the afternoon and the junction (*parvan-sandhi*)—

On the previous day (pūrvedyuḥ), even in the absence of the fourth part of the *parvan*, the sacrifice must be performed during the third part of the *parvan*; and on the following day (pareyuḥ), even in the absence of the three initial parts of the *pratipad*, the sacrifice must be performed during the fourth part.
This alternative (vikalpa) resulting from the force of the injunction for performance cannot be prevented even by the gods.

[The opponent claims: "And exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is not the primary meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), but rather it is [its meaning] through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). by this same logic, even in the case of a prohibition (*niṣedha*), the sacrifice would occur on the previous day's portion.

For, due to the impossibility [of otherwise], the sacrifice would otherwise result in being optionally performed during either the fourth part of the previous day or the first part of the following day.
"One should not sacrifice in the fourth part," because the performance of the sacrifice has been prohibited in the first quarter of the fourfold division.

Otherwise, since it would follow that one might take *māṣa* beans as a substitute for *mudga* beans, Jaimini stated in the sixth chapter: "It is either prohibited by specific [rule], or the Vedic text [prescribes] what is sought";

Because [the performance] is possible at that time; nor should it be said that the concluding statement (*upasaṃhāra*) is made by the words "of the first day of the lunar fortnight" (*śrādyāḥ pratipadasya*), for there is no contradiction since this [phrase] indicates other times, and thus it is untenable for it to be intended as a concluding statement.

Since there is no such defect if it refers to the junction occurring in the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), it is logical that it should indeed refer to that.

therefore, since the prescribed time is impossible at that [latter] point, the sacrifice must take place right then. On this point, some say that when the moon is visible on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad), the performance of the *iṣṭi* should be understood as optional; for if the New Moon sacrifice (*darśayāga*) is prohibited solely because the moon is seen even though the first day occurs in the morning, then [the following applies].

In this way, the statement of Kātyāyana would be entirely inconsistent in meaning; for, by the rule "if the second [lunar day] is cited," having prescribed the *anyādhāna* on the fourteenth day, it follows by implication that it is performed on the fifteenth day at the appropriate time.

If it were said that the Soma sacrifice should take place on the second day, the first lunar day (*pratipad*), which is the day for sacrificing, that would be improper; because that [day] is not suitable for sacrifice, and due to the force of the text regarding the days preceding it, it is stated: "In that case, one should give water mixed with *vyāhṛti* mantras to a twice-born person"—thus, in the absence of the sacrifice, there is the *vyāhṛti*.

[The opponent] strikes [this point] with these words: "Otherwise, it would be [merely] for the sake of praise (*arthavāda*). That is incorrect. The notion that "this is some kind of conceptual construction" is already largely refuted by this very point. Because of the aforementioned fault in the first case; in the second case, even the cognition that the new-moon day is the occasion for the appearance of the moon is sublated. Therefore, like the appearance of the moon, the prohibition of fire is not occasional.

When it is said, "He sees with the eye," it is understood that he does not see with the right [eye]. It must be accepted that this is a *guṇavāda* (a figurative statement). Because of this statement, some say: "This is not tenable; for instance, it cannot be restricted that only the Taittirīyakas perform the *parvan* [rites], since the *parvan-anvākhyāna-karman* is also performed by other *caraṇas*."

Because of the injunction. Nor can the meaning of the sentence be understood as "only those who have committed a transgression should perform the *upākarma* on a day other than the *parvan*," for that would entail a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to the reference to a qualified subject; furthermore, since such specific qualifications have not been previously established, it is impossible to refer to them. And this being so with respect to the qualified ritual act—
Because the injunction for the Taittirīyakas is untenable; for it is the agent who is enjoined to the ritual act, not the agent in relation to the act.
Furthermore, the *upākarma* and its time—the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*)—are prescribed by the other [branch] only for those very [Taittirīyakas].
Therefore, that injunction is found in the *Mātrākārikā*; here, however, it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the *Paurṇamāsī* [sacrifice].
The section concerning the time for the *upākarma* ceremony. And here, a connection with the time of the *audgrabhaṇa* is indicated. In that regard, if by the Taittirīyakas—
If another relationship of the *kalpa* is then indicated, the sentence becomes divided due to the mention of two relationships.
Furthermore, the Taittirīyaka authors are themselves merely auxiliary (*aṅga*), and there is no mutual relationship between auxiliaries.
It does not exist. Nor should it be said that, according to the principle of the "ruddy one-year-old cow" (*aruṇaikahāyanī*), there is a connection of the qualities at the end of the five [steps];
for in that case, a purchase qualified by the substance—the one-year-old cow—characterized by the quality of redness is enjoined.
Subsequently, because the substance and the quality mutually require one another and possess a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇatva*), they are connected. However, here...
It occurs. Furthermore, in this *kārikā*, there is no injunction for the *upākarma* rite.

Nor is there grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—even in the sense of substance and attribute—between the *parva* and the *vaitānika-taittirīyaka*, because they lack mutual expectancy. Therefore, the word *taittirīyaka* is intended to signify the *vidhāna* (injunction) itself; being an *upalakṣaṇa* (an indicative term), it serves to include [the entire context].

According to the principle of the section on different recensions (*śākhāntarādhikaraṇa*), the rule for the *upākarma* ceremony applies to all schools (*sarva-śākhā*). Since there is no contradiction, the specific modification (*upada-vikṛtatva*) prescribed for the Taittirīyas should also be adopted by others. Thus it is ordained in the *Pariśiṣṭa*:
That which has been declared by the teachers of the Veda as being non-contradictory to other scriptures should be performed by the learned,
just like the Agnihotra and other such rites.

Since the statement beginning with “The Śrāvaṇī [full moon] wards off difficulties” does not specify a particular ritual act (*karmaviśeṣa*), its subject matter is the investiture of the *pavitra* by Hiraṇyagarbha, as well as the *Śrāvaṇī-karman* which is an ancillary part of the *Upākarma* and is performed for the sake of prosperity (*ābhyudayika*). Therefore, for the Taittirīyas alone, the *Udavasānīya* sacrifice is the *Parvan-upākarma*.

[The opponent says: "It is logical. [The author replies: That is illogical. However, where there is no other possible recourse (*ananyagatipada*), there the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) is the objective (*uddeśya*) for fear of the redundancy of the word, as in "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa of eight years," and so forth. But in the case of both words [in the present context], it is merely for the purpose of dispelling the misconception that the two words together constitute the cause for the offering (*havirārtti*) of the Āgneya sacrifice due to its priority.

There is no alternative recourse for the words, nor is there a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), because that [split] occurs only when one intends to express a qualification of the subject (*uddeśya-viśeṣaṇa*). Indeed,
in the case of the desire for the four aims (*caturvarga-kāma*) and the determination of time by means of residue (*pariśeṣataḥ*), [there is no such split].

But it is not in reference to a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭoddeśa*). This has been explained at length by Bhavadeva: "In the case of one who objects here, a rebuttal must be formulated by resorting to a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), because that [objection] is to be accepted. Furthermore, since the previously cited statement from the *Vārttika* establishes that the mention of the *parvan* is a restatement (*anuvāda*) based on the attainment of the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, this applies to the ritual action as well.

The injunction regarding the agent is appropriate because an injunction has as its domain that which is not already established. Nor does the injunction of two relations result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), because it relies upon an injunction of a qualified whole (*viśiṣṭavidhi*); otherwise, the distinction between different authors of texts would be abandoned, and consequently, all [distinctions] would be undermined. Furthermore, if this were not accepted, the figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) would be rendered purposeless.

The two would not be mere restatements (*anuvāda*). If it is argued: "Just as in the case of 'One should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva,' where, due to the risk of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), the word *vaiśvadeva* is applied by secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) according to the principle of 'the fit' (*icinyāya*) to the sacrifices already under discussion—so too, here, one should accept [the injunction] even at the cost of the complexity of a qualified injunction. [Response: No.

For even there, figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is absent. Indeed, the application of the word *vaiśvadeva* does not proceed from its connection with the Viśvedevas as deities, but rather from its connection with the Viśvedevas as performers [of the sacrifice]. Thus it is heard in the Taittirīyaka: "When the Viśvedevas sacrificed, that is the *vaiśvadevatva* of the Vaiśvadeva"; this refers to the application of the term found in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

The status of being a secondary indicator (*nimitta*) applies everywhere, as in such cases as "because they ran toward it (*ājimoyus*), therefore the *ājya* offerings are called *ājya*," and so forth. As for the mention of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), that is rejected because it would lead to a lack of systematic order if one were to accept figurative usage based on mere acceptance [of a primary sense] while simultaneously treating it as a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*). Furthermore, there is prolixity (*gaurava*) in that case regarding the qualified injunction.

Furthermore, the assumption that there is an extension (*atideśa*) from another ritual action serves a purpose for the restatement (*anuvāda*). In this case, there is a difference: in the case of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), there is merely the burden of complexity (*gaurava*); however, in its absence, there is a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), whereas a purposeless restatement is [unacceptable]. Moreover, in a qualified injunction, the simultaneous connection (*pārṣṇikasambandha*) of the various qualities is logically established, and it is for the sake of performing the ritual action that the agent [is enjoined].

There certainly exists an expectancy for a specific time. Nor does the principle of the *śākhān-karādhikaraṇa* apply here; for if the performance [of the Śrāvaṇa sacrifice] were already established for others by the rule "They should perform the Śrāvaṇa at the full moon of the month of Śrāvaṇa," it would follow that the word "Taittirīyaka" is redundant. Furthermore, being governed by the full moon (*parvādhikatva*) is not specifically enjoined in the Taittirīya *Gṛhya-sūtra*. And if...
In the *Kālikāpurāṇa*, it is stated that one should sustain the self that has departed; this is the concealment (*tirodhāna*) even of those who have transcended [the world].
The determination of the time for the *utsarjana* (concluding rite) follows the established practice.

Since the *upākarma* (commencement rite) occurs on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, for the Bahvṛcas as well, the *upākarma* should take place at that very same time, as stated in the scriptural injunctions.
However, upon careful consideration, it is the same in that they both resort to a different time [for the sacrifice].

Furthermore, in this way, even the word *va* (or) would be unintended, because the aforementioned objection regarding the interpretation of the word *taittirīya* applies equally there as well. Therefore, the settled rule is this: when, on a single day, the *parvan* overlaps with the time for the ritual (*karmakāla*).

Then, when the Upākarma for all [schools] does not span the ritual time (*karmakāla*) on both days, the Taittirīyas perform the Upākarma on the first day of the fortnight (*parvan*), while others do so on the other [day]. Regarding this,
Yājñavalkya says:
Now follows the time for the ritual dismissal (utsarjana) of the Vedas:
On the Rohiṇī asterism in the month of Pauṣa, or likewise on the Aṣṭakā day,
one should perform the formal dismissal of the Vedic scriptures at the water’s edge according to the prescribed rule.

On the Rohiṇī asterism or the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, one should perform the Utsarjana (the ritual suspension) of the Vedas outside the village in the vicinity of water;

the meaning is that one should now abandon the method by which the study was conducted from the Upākarma onwards, but not entirely. For this very reason, Manu states [this] immediately after the Utsarjana.
A twice-born man should perform the *bandasā* rite under the Puṣya asterism,
or he may perform the early release (*acir-utsarjana*) on the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha during the forenoon.
If the commencement of the study period (*upākarma*) takes place in Śrāvaṇa, then the conclusion (*utsarjana*) occurs on the first day of the bright fortnight of Puṣya during the forenoon;
however, when it occurs in Proṣṭhapada, it means [the conclusion] is in Māgha, because of the rule: "One should study for four and a half months."
Baudhāyana says that one should bring a full water-pot from the eastern or northern direction and release that water upon it.
Bhrājasvamin says [the same].
In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, in the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa*, in the section on the determination of rites (*Karmaviniścaya*),

In this regard, Rohiṇī is the first [lunar day] of the month of Pauṣa according to the statement of Yājñavalkya. Kātyāyana says: "Then, during the northern solstice, one who knows the Dharma should study."
The time for their disposal is either at the full moon of Āśvayuja or at that of Proṣṭhapada.
Regarding the time for the suspension (*utsarjana*) according to the *Chandogas*, Gārgya says:

In the *Pariśiṣṭa*: "If, in the month of Proṣṭhapada, [the moon] should be in Puṣya or in a nakṣatra preceding Hasta,
then on that Śravaṇa day, the twice-born should perform the formal abandonment (utsarga) of the Vedic texts."
It should be made of Khadira wood. One should perform the Utsarjana (the ritual conclusion) under the Puṣya asterism, or on the day of the Upākarma;
and these two rites must be performed every year.
As Kātyāyana said: "The annual *upākarma* ceremony, along with the *utsarga*, which is performed according to rule on occasions of prosperity—
by that, there shall be a restoration of the *chandas*."
Whatever rite is performed by the twice-born with unimpaired Vedic meters,
even while they are merely playing, that always brings them success.

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Determination of Time" (*Kālanirṇaya*), in the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, in its supplement (*pariśeṣakhaṇḍa*), composed by the illustrious Hemādri— the sovereign over all kings, the great king of kings, the consort of the illustrious Mahādevī, the lord of all [learning], and the master of all branches of knowledge.

In the *Brahmavaivarta*: "O twice-born one, hear from me their twelve names alone:
one is named Viṣṇupada, and likewise Ṣaḍaśītimukha."
The equinox is the third, and there are two others, the southern and the northern.

There are two solstices, two equinoxes, and four [other] transits;
these twelve, beginning with the movement of Viṣṇu’s foot, are the transitions.

Libra and Virgo are at the equinox (viṣuvat); the others follow between those two.

"Between those two," that is, between Capricorn (makara) and Cancer (karkaṭa), "at the equinoxes. In some places, the reading is "tato'parā golamadhye," where "gola" refers to the zodiacal circle (rāśicakra).
[The six aśītis occur] in Sagittarius, Gemini, Virgo, and Pisces.
In the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra): In Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, Capricorn, and Aquarius, there is the Viṣṇupadī and the Latā [yogas]. Likewise:

The equinoxes (viṣuva) occur at Libra and Aries; the six signs of Pisces, Virgo, Gemini, and Sagittarius are the "sixty-four" (ṣaḍaśīti); the solstices (ayana) occur at Capricorn and Cancer; and in the remaining signs, it is Viṣṇupadī.

In the *Devīpurāṇa*, seven designations for each [solar transit] are stated by means of their specific conjunctions with the constellations: "She (the year) should be understood as sevenfold, though she is indeed one; listen to how each single transit, such as Aries and the rest, is sevenfold—of seven kinds.
Listen to the manner in which each individual transit, beginning with Aries, is sevenfold.
O King, the sevenfold *saṃkrānti* is said to be composed of the *rākṣasa* [element] mixed with the *manda*, *mandākinī*, *dhvāṅkṣa*, *ghorā*, and *mahodarī*.
On Sunday, [the demon] Ghorā; on Monday, Dhvāṅkṣa; on Tuesday, Mahodara.
The Chapter on the Transits of the Planets:
When Mercury is present, it is named Mandākinī; when Jupiter, it is Mandā.
Mixed with Śukravāra, Khā, and Rācasau on Prameśvara—
these are the seven Saṃkrāntis, and their fruit is likewise declared.

One should know that *mandā* is characterized by specific qualities in the *bhuṣa* [meters], while *mandākinī* is likewise gentle; *ciprā* is to be understood as having upward-moving limbs, and it is proclaimed as *udhaurā*.
Mahodara should be known by its movements; it is predominantly rājasa, yet it is also specified as being mixed when occurring at the junctions (saṃkrama).

The "heavy" (bhuvāṇi) [nakṣatras] are Śravaṇa, Uttarā-phalgunī, Uttarā-bhādrapadā, and Rohiṇī. The "middling" (mhadūmi) are Anurādhā, Citrā, Revatī, and Mṛgaśīrṣa. The "light" (laghūni) are Abhijit, Hasta, Aśvinī, and Puṣya.
The "rising" (udyāṇi) are the three Pūrvās and Bharaṇī and Maghā. The "movable" (carāṇi) are Punarvasu...

and [the numbers] four, five, seven, eight, nine, and twelve [are associated with these].

In this manner, according to the respective enumeration, seven periods (*kāla*) are to be observed during all transits (*saṃkrānti*). Thus concludes the determination regarding the birds. Now, concerning the lack of knowledge regarding the birds, there is the *Sāṃvatsarika* and the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*.
The Determination of the Time for Śrāvakas.
Aruṇa said:

O Lord of the Immortals, how can a highly wise man who does not know the direction, the object, or even the month of his deceased parents perform the *śrāddha* for them according to the rules throughout the year?

In this context, "of the parents" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for others as well, because the same practice is observed when the specific date of the Śrāddha or the anniversary is unknown.
Āditya said:
O son of Vinatā, that man who does not know the anniversary of my death—
The Section on Determining the Time for Śrāddha: O King, one should perform the annual śrāddha on the new moon day (amāvāsyā).

The meaning is that for one who has died— whether he was away from home or not— if the lunar day (tithi) is unknown but the month is known, the annual rite (sāṃvatsarika) should be performed on the new moon (amāvāsyā) of that month.
Thus said Gṛhaspati:
If it is not known whether [the person] has died, perished, or is away on a journey,
then the anniversary of death should be observed at the end of the month from which he was last heard of.

"In that [case]," on the new moon day of that month, "on the anniversary of death"—the remainder of the sentence being "whatever is to be performed there"; "having gone abroad" is an indicative mark for the cause of ignorance [of the date].
Thus, it is said in the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
Even when those two [the father and son] are separated without the father being on a journey,
at that time as well, both are entitled to the rites for the deceased day, just as before.
Regarding this very subject,
Marīci states that when an obstacle to the śrāddha arises and the [proper] day is unknown,
it should be performed on the eleventh day, especially during the dark fortnight.

By the phrase "especially on the dark fortnight" (*kṛṣṇapakṣe viśeṣataḥ*), it is understood that the dark fortnight is being emphasized because of its superior merit. Consequently, when the eleventh day of the bright fortnight (*śuklaikādaśī*) is obtained as an alternative (*vikalpa*), it is thus [to be followed].

When the month and the fortnight (pakṣa) are known, but the lunar day (tithi) is not known, the Śrāddha should be performed on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) situated within that very fortnight, because there is no reason to abandon the known fortnight. When even the fortnight is not known, it should be performed on any eleventh day; in its absence—
Also in the Kādambarī and in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "That man who knows only the day but not the month..."
In the section on the determination of time within the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Caturmacintāmaṇi*:
"One should perform it either in Mārgaśīrṣa, or in Bhādrapada, or in Māgha."
Especially for one who always worships me as a patron (bhojaka).
But for one whose day of death is known, yet not the month— in that case, the *śrāddha* should be performed on that day, whether it be in Mārgaśīrṣa, Bhādrapada, or Māgha.
Thus says Bṛhaspati:
If the month is not known, but the day alone is known,
then that day should be taken as falling in either the month of Mārgaśīrṣa or Māgha.
But when both the day and the month of one who has gone abroad are unknown,
then the annual rite (sāṃvatsarika) should be performed on the day and month corresponding to the time of his departure;
thus he himself says:
When the day and month of death are not known, however,
the day and month of departure should be taken according to the previously mentioned method.

In all instances, by the word *dina* (day), the lunar day (*tithi*) is to be understood. The meaning of the phrase "by the aforementioned method" is as follows: when the specific lunar day is unknown and the month is known, the annual rite (*sāṃvatsarika*) is performed on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) occurring within that month. When the lunar day is known but the month is unknown, it is performed in either the month of Mārgaśīrṣa or Māgha.

One should perform it on that very lunar day (tithi). However, if both the lunar day and the month of departure are unknown, one should perform it on the lunar day and month at the time when news of his death was heard.
Thus said Pracetas:
"In the case of full knowledge [of the time of death], it should be on the new moon day or on the day of the Śravaṇā asterism.
"On the day of the Śravaṇā" means on the lunar day when news of the death is heard.
This is also stated in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
The noble Āryācī delivered the news of their death, exactly as previously stated.
The section on the determination of the division of shares.
Regarding the investigation of the lunar day of Śravaṇa, in the practice of the Māva-cāra and the two paths of the Tantrāya, there is the absence of all [obstacles].

The annual [observance] should be performed on the same lunar day in either Mārgaśīrṣa or Māgha, for the purpose of causing [the Dharma] to be heard, for transformation, and to prevent forgetfulness. Regarding the determination of the lunar day for both hearing and transformation, it should be done in Mārgaśīrṣa or on the new moon day of the dark fortnight.
Thus it has been said regarding its power:
"One does not know whether [the deceased] is dead or even alive in any way whatsoever;
therefore, one should perform the Śrāddha rite for them on the new moon day in the month of Māgha or Mārgaśīrṣa."

"In any way whatsoever" (*kathañcana*) means that [the news] is not perceived by any means at all, such as news of death. However, in the case of one who has gone abroad, if there is no news of his death nor even news of his life, and there is no arrival for eight years (*padmavarṣa*), then after that time, the purification through the *pālāśa* leaves is indeed useless.

Having fashioned an image of the body and performed the cremation rites according to the prescribed rules, one should then perform the annual anniversary rite (*sāṃvatsarika*) on the day marked by the same lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), the same lunar fortnight (*pakṣa*), and the same lunar date (*tithi*). Thus said Jātūkarṇya.
While the father is away on a journey, one should live with his mother; one should not consume even a drop of liquor.
After fifteen years have passed, one may adopt a substitute for him.
Then, one should perform his consecration according to the prescribed rule;
thereafter, one should perform all the Śiva-rites beginning with that [consecration].
Thus ends the determination regarding the *sāṃsarika* crow in the *Bābāparidhāna*.
In the *Bābūpurāṇa*, here follows the determination regarding the *maghā-śrāddha*.
Performing śrāddha rites on the Maṣā days, one shall obtain all desires.
In the fourth chapter, concerning the determination of time as a supplement to that which is produced by reflection:
"By him, the ancestors are always worshipped as if they were directly present."
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who performs the Śrāddha on the Maghā constellation:
his ancestors are satisfied, and he shall have a continuous lineage.
By this very yoga, O King, those who give clothing, a dwelling, and sandals,
and especially food, during a śrāddha performed under the Maghā nakṣatra,
their ancestors remain satisfied for thirteen years.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather,
gaze upon the son who has been born, just as birds eye a peepul tree.
"With honey, meat, rhinoceros flesh, milk, and milk-rice—
this man will offer us the śrāddha during the rainy season under the Maghā asterism."
By giving according to the prescribed rite under the Maghā asterism, one obtains four boons;
the ancestors, when honored, bestow wealth, food, sons, and long life.

Likewise, that which is given in Bhādra, Danta, and Padma becomes equal to a thousand niṣkas.
"Whether they are divided or undivided, they should always perform the *śrāddha*;
however, other than during the *Maghā* [nakṣatra], there is no entitlement for the eldest brother alone.
Thus says Vasiṣṭha.
"They grieve for one who gives curd that has not been touched by a cow's hoof, as well as various kinds of [other gifts], during the rainy season and the month of Māgha. Thus [it is said].
[Chapter 11] Section on the Determination of the Time for Śrāddha. These statements refer to śrāddhas that are devoid of the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa). And so it is said:
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa there is this statement:
"O Bhārata, by fasting on the day of Saṃkrānti and by performing the ritual breaking of the fast (pāraṇa),
as well as by the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍadāna), the eldest son perishes."
And so it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "For one performing a Śrāddha on the Maghā [nakṣatra], the eldest son perishes;
likewise, fasting during a solar or lunar eclipse, or at the time of a saṃkrānti [solar transit]."

As for the citation from the Purāṇa regarding the essence of conduct, which states, "By giving a gift of cloth during the Maghā-Ardrā [nakṣatra], one obtains four boons," that refers to a subject other than a householder who has sons.
Others, however, say: this is merely a prohibition against the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) alone; that is possible.
And so it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"Only a funeral ball (*piṇḍa*) should be offered in the absence of wealth and a wife;
however, when the *śrāddha* occasions arrive, one should perform them even if one is fasting."
But surely, let the prohibition apply to both cases as well, since it is improper to invalidate multiple scriptural injunctions.
Therefore, the *maghā-śrāddha* should also be performed with the *sapiṇḍana* rite. That is incorrect;
because there is no reason for a definitive choice between them, the prohibition applies to both.
Others, however, say: "The *trayodaśī-śrāddha*, the seasonal *śrāddhas*, and even the *maghā-śrāddha*—all belonging to a single ancestral group (*ekavarga*)—are prohibited.

This is incorrect. For that [prohibition] has been shown by the force of such scriptural statements as, "One should commence the *śrāddha* for a single group on the *trayodaśī*," whereas here there is an absence of such a statement.

If it is argued that [the prohibition] applies because of its logical equivalence, [we reply: no, for the prohibition "one should not perform a *śrāddha* with a weaver, a potter, or a *kāpālika*" is appropriately understood as referring to *sapiṇḍa-śrāddhas*. Furthermore, it is heard in scripture that "a son attains greatness through the offering of a peacock's feather," but this does not refer to the performance of a *śrāddha*, since the obligation to perform such [specific rites] has already been demonstrated.
Thus concludes the determination regarding the *māsa-śrāddha*.
The determination of the time for the *śrāddha* on the occasion of the four-month anniversary and other such events,
as well as the determination of the time for the *śrāddha* on the occasions of purification from impurity (*prāyaścitta*) and so forth, has been concluded.
Now follows that [determination].
When impurity arises due to the death of a deity, purification does not occur;
only when that period of impurity has passed is the śrāddha offered to them.

The meaning is that if impurity (āśauca) arises for those entitled to perform the Śrāddha before the commencement of the primary time, then— whether because the primary time is near at hand or because it has been defiled by impurity— the ancestral rite (paitṛka-karma) must be performed immediately after the period of impurity has passed.
Regarding the statement:
"If that [day] should be defiled by anyone through birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or the like,
one should perform it again on that very same day immediately after the *sūtaka* has ended."

Regarding that, when a *śrāddha* is defiled by *sūtaka* (impurity due to birth), the view that one should perform it immediately after the *sūtaka* is not at all inconsistent with the statement of Dubbaśṛṅga. Furthermore, as for the alternative view that it may be performed on that very same day, this refers to the primary time [of the occasion] when other obstacles—indicated by words such as "again" (*punaḥ*) or "on that very day"—have been removed; thus, it should be understood as a rule consistent with the aforementioned statements.
This is another view; however, this alternative method concerns the *atimāsika* (intercalary month) *śrāddha* performed according to the lunar day (*tithi*).
This is because, in that case, even in the absence of contact with the specific month, the lunar day itself is accepted as the time for performance.
For this very reason, Devala says:
If an obstacle should arise when the Ekoddiṣṭa has arrived,
one should first perform the Śrāddha on that same lunar day (tithi) in another month.
"In this [next] month," meaning in the month immediately following; "on that lunar day," meaning on the anniversary of the date of death;

the meaning is that one should perform the *śrāddha* for those who have passed away due to obstacles during that fortnight (whether bright or dark) in which they were remembered. Regarding the phrase "if there is an obstacle," here too, in order not to contradict the statement of Saṃvarta, it refers to causes other than ritual impurity (*āśauca*).
