The remainder is to be understood as follows: even in the case of the monthly *śrāddha*, when it arises without the cause of impurity (*aśauca*), the performance of the *śrāddha* immediately after the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) should be followed according to the statement of Śrī Vyāsaśṛṅga.
For this very reason, Devakhāmin also stated: "This statement of Vyāsaśṛṅga [applies] to the impurity of birth..."

Vyāsa states that this refers to a different occasion, for there is a statement from another *Smṛti* regarding its suspension on that very day: "If a death occurs when an *ekoddiṣṭa* ceremony has arrived," and so forth.
Thus says Vyāsa.
"When an obstacle arises for a Śrāddha, or if one dies in the interim during a period of birth or death impurity,
some wise men say that one should perform the Śrāddha on the New Moon day."

Regarding the phrase "death or birth occurring in the interval": this refers to when a *sūtaka* (impurity due to childbirth) or *mṛtaka* (impurity due to death) occurs during the performance of a *śrāddha*, prior to the commencement of the cooking. Some maintain that this refers to the annual *śrāddha* performed after the *uddharaṇa* (the setting aside of food) on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). That is incorrect.
When the monthly anniversary has arrived, but an impurity due to death or birth occurs in the interim,
the wise declare that the rite should be performed with *darbha* grass at that very time.

Since the rule for even a one-month [observance] is established by the expression "limited duration," the mention of the new moon day (amāvāsyā) is an elliptical indication for the eleventh day of the bright fortnight (śukla-ekādaśī) and the eleventh day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇa-ekādaśī). For this very reason, Marīci says:
When the specific details of a *śrāddha* have arisen but the day of death remains unknown,
it should be performed on the eleventh day, especially during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*).

The grammatical connection is: "especially on that which is the eleventh day of the dark fortnight. Since the dark fortnight alone is used for ancestral rites (*piṭakārya*) because it brings about maturation (*pācana*), it should be understood—according to the logic of the *daṇḍāpūpa* maxim—that even the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) occurring after the dark eleventh day is superior for ancestral rites. Here, the subsequent time...
It is the most excellent because it is proximate to the primary time; it is pleasant to behold for those who see it, as it is free from defects.
In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, in the section on the determination of time (*pariśeṣakālanirṇaya*),
it should be understood that this is because of the existence of both truth and falsehood. And so it has been stated there as well:
"The gift should be given by one who has become pure;

that lunar day (tithi) which is attained [by him] is the one for which the rite must be performed, and never any other. This is the meaning: first, the gift should be given by one who is possessed of purity; therefore, when such auspicious times occur, it is possible [to perform the rite].

The lunar day (*tithi*) that follows immediately is what "occurs" (*apratipadyate*), and it should be understood as being an integral part of the rite to be performed; no other convenient lunar day is to be used, nor should one defiled by impurity (*āśauca*) ever be undertaken. He states that the primary lunar day, when not defiled by impurity, is always to be observed.

"One should not interrupt the lunar day (tithi) due to impurity arising from death occurring by chance; the ancestral rite (pārvaṇa śrāddha) must be offered, and one should certainly not cause a break [in the sequence]. Here, "by chance" means according to one's own will. When there is an interruption of the day of death due to death or birth-impurity (mṛta-sūtaka), that [interruption] is to be disregarded.

It has been stated that the *śrāddha* should be performed upon the cessation of one's own impurity (*āśauca*). However, because of the rule regarding the invitation at the commencement [of the rite], this must be done only before the impurity is known, and not at a later time.
Thus, it is said in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
When the Brahmins have been invited and the Śrāddha rite has commenced—
indeed, from the moment of inviting a Brahmin who is devoted to the study of the Vedas and other such duties.
Even while the ancestors remain within the body, no impurity (āśauca) exists at all for either the giver or the receiver,
whether in the case of birth (sūtaka) or death (mṛtaka).
There shall never be any fault in cases such as funeral offerings (śrāddha) when [the impurity] is unknown;
however, once it is known, the performance of expiation and other rites shall fall solely upon the eater.
The giver of food perishes when someone,
being composed, discards the remainder of that [food] as leavings.
The Section on the Time for Taking Food. Having sipped water with water belonging to another, the twice-born become pure.
If an impurity (sūtaka) occurs between a marriage and a sacrifice, others should provide the remaining food; this is what has been declared.

This, however, refers to births and deaths other than those occurring in the context of giving and enjoying. In the case of "the giver shall not be touched by [the sin of] enjoyment," there is a specific fault [involved].
Regarding the one who performs the rite:
there is no fault in giving wealth that was previously intended for the purpose.
This has been stated concerning the qualified person defiled by impurity (āśauca), when the primary time has passed due to that impurity.

The *śrāddha* must be performed upon the cessation [of the impurity]. Since the householder has the right to perform it only together with his wife, when she is defiled by the impurity resulting from the appearance of menses, he must bypass the primary time and perform the *śrāddha* only after the cessation of that impurity.

Hoshana states that when the time for the *āmāśrāddha* has arrived, it must be performed by the lord of the *rajasālā* alone, even if he is solitary. Furthermore, [he says] this applies to one who is traveling abroad with his wife, or whose wife is in her menses.
"One should not perform [a śrāddha] with prepared food; it is ordained that for one who has invited [the guests], it shall be done with raw grain.
Having thus introduced a partial exception to the rule regarding the śrāddha with raw grain, Hārīta states:
"In the event of an obstacle to a śrāddha for the twice-born, a śrāddha with raw grain is prescribed."

"A month that has passed since the new moon day [is considered] after a year. Thus, when an obstacle to the *śrāddha*—such as the appearance of menses in one's wife—has arisen, it is proclaimed that the *śrāddha* must be performed; this refers specifically to the time of the new moon and so forth, but not to the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*).
The meaning is that even the annual [offering] should be performed; however, it must be performed without causing any harm [to the recipient].

And that [is done] by means of a single portion, because there is no sin in defiling the wife of one who possesses great authority, as there is an absence of [such] impurity due to the intervention of another [wife].

In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, in the section on the determination of time (*Kālanirṇaya*) within the *Paricchedakhaṇḍa* [11th Paṭala], it is stated that [the rite] must be performed precisely at the time when the obstacle in the form of the appearance [of the menses] has ceased. As it is said in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*:
"A woman who has bathed on the fourth day shall become purified from her menstrual flow."
In rites for the gods and for the ancestors, one becomes pure on the fifth day.
In another authoritative text:
"When the day of death has arrived and the woman is in her menses, the śrāddha should not be performed then; one should have it performed on the fifth day."

However, for one who has taken another wife while still possessing the requisite qualification (*adhikāra*), since that qualification has not lapsed, the rite must be performed at the primary time itself.
Regarding one who is unable to perform the *āmam-śrāddha* (funeral rite with raw food), he prescribes the *hema-śrāddha* (funeral rite with gold).
In the absence of materials, in the absence of twice-born priests, during travel, upon the birth of a son,
or when one's wife is in her menses, one should perform a Hema-śrāddha (a śrāddha with gold).
Only the substance to be eaten is intended to be prepared; one should eat during the day.
This concludes the determination of the times for *śrāddha* on occasions such as periods of impurity (*āśauca*).
Now, specific types of *śrāddha* are prescribed for the morning, forenoon, midday, and afternoon.

Since evening time is prohibited, as it is with other [specific] actions, this section concerning the eastern and western directions is commenced for the sake of discerning those times. In that regard, by the power of the term *yoga* (connection/junction), it is understood quite clearly that the first part is the "forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇa*) and the latter part is the "afternoon" (*aparāhṇa*).
And so Manu says:
"Just as the latter fortnight is distinguished from the former fortnight by its initial days,
even so the afternoon is distinguished from the forenoon."

The Section on the Restraint of Time and Place for the Śrāddha Rite.
Regarding the *manmatha-śrāddha*, it is stated that the distinction between "forenoon" (*pūrvāhṇa*) and "afternoon" (*aparāhṇa*) is based on the Vaiśya; however,
this does not mean that the division of the day into parts designates the first portion as "forenoon" and the latter portion as "afternoon."

As for the word "path" (*lam*): it is now explained. When a day is divided, there are two parts, the prior and the posterior halves; these two have not been mentioned here [as such]. Furthermore, even though they lack formal similarity (*asārūpya*), the fact that the day is divided implies that its prior and posterior portions are designated as "the first half" (*pūrvāhṇa*) and "the second half" (*aparāhṇa*). And that—

Because it is appropriate for something to serve as an illustration based on similarity even through mere specific distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*). True; nevertheless, because the parts are not taken up [as the subject] and in order to conform to total similarity, the cognition of the intended division arises. This must be accepted in this way so that there may be no contradiction with the *tara* suffix. Now, in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*— [The text ends here.]

Whether [the term] is divided into two or four parts according to the expressions for divisions of the day, let the division based on etymological derivation (*yaugika*), similarity to examples (*dṛṣṭāntasārūpya*), and conceptual construction (*kalpanāmūlaka*) be set aside. True; however, that which is technical (*pāribhāṣika*), being taught by the word "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*), is stronger than both the etymological and the conceptual due to its lack of occasion (*anavakāśatva*) and its status as direct perception (*pratyakṣatva*).

Obstruction would indeed arise from [the word] itself; however, for the very purpose of preventing the obstruction of the etymological meaning by means of a technical rule (paribhāṣā), even that meaning derived through etymology has been defined as such in the Skanda Purāṇa.
"The first part is until the *śrāvartana*, and after that comes the *aparāhna*.
Thus, *śrāvartana* is the middle of the day; having divided the day into two parts, it is said that the second portion [is *aparāhna*].

One view is that [the day] is [divided into] three parts. Now, another view is stated regarding the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) as one of the three divisions of the day: "The forenoon indeed belongs to the gods, the midday to men, and the afternoon to the ancestors;
therefore, one gives [the offering] in the afternoon. And furthermore—

The Śruti, having determined the five muhūrta-measured portions of the day consisting of *hartas*—namely, the *pūrvāhṇa*, *madhyāhna*, and so forth—assigns them respectively to the ritual acts of *eva*, *mānu*, and *paiḍhaka*. This is what is understood [from the text]. Furthermore, regarding the *pārvaṇaśrāddha* prescribed for the time of the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*)...

In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, within the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* and the section on the determination of time (*Kālanirṇaya*), in the third part, the instruction regarding what must be performed by a human being will be shown in the section on the application of time (*Kālaniyoga-prakaraṇa*).
That too is divided into three parts; the third part is the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), as seen from the observation of other scriptural meanings.
It should not be overlooked: the view is that when [the debt] is divided into three parts, the third part constitutes the interest (*aparādha*).
Alternatively, another view holds that when divided into four parts by unequal portions, the third part constitutes the interest. And so says Gobhila:
"The forenoon consists of one and a half *praharas*, likewise midday consists of one *prahara*,
the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) extends up to the third [part], and the evening (*sāyāhna*) is beyond that.
Here, the portion of the day measured as one and a half *praharas* starting from sunrise is the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*).

The period above that, measuring one *mahara* (three hours), is midday (*madhyāhna*). Above that, until the completion of the third *prahara*, measuring half a *prahara*, is afternoon (*aparāhṇa*). Above that, for the duration of one *prahara*, is evening (*sāyāhna*)—this is the meaning.
Thus, it is the opinion that the third part of the day, divided into four parts, is afternoon (*aparāhṇa*). In this regard:

Another opinion holds that when [the year] is divided fivefold into equal parts, the fourth part is *aparā* (the afternoon). Regarding this, there is the Śatapatha Śruti: "The sun indeed is everything.
When he rises, that is spring; when he is at the time of the cows gathering (*saṅgava*), that is summer; when it is midday, that is the rainy season."
Then there is *thadāparāc*, then *śaraccadaiva* at sunset, and then *hemanta*.

Thus, when a day measured by fifteen *muhūrtas* is divided into five parts, there arise the five periods beginning with morning (*prātar*), each limited by three [muhūrtas]. In this regard, although...
Therefore, immediately after the statement that [the study] should be undertaken at midday alone,

there is heard a fivefold division as a supplementary element (*śeṣa*) to the injunction for midday, in connection with the designation of the time-period following right after that; nevertheless, it is to be relied upon (*upajīvya*) as that which makes known the duration of the time required by the rites prescribed for the morning and other periods.

If it is argued that even when the prohibition applies to a *śrāddha* performed on an auspicious occasion (*nimittaka-śrāddha*), there would follow the undesirable consequence that no *vṛddhi-śrāddha* could be performed at the birth of a son after the [previous] *śrāddha*, and therefore the contradiction with established practice (*ācāra*) pertains to occasions other than those;
we say no. For otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that no *śrāddha* could be performed during a solar eclipse, which would contradict the practice of former authorities.
It might be argued that [the Smṛti] has a subject matter distinct from that [of the Śruti]. This is not so;
for since there exist injunctions regarding ancestral rites (śrāddha) that have different causes but are simultaneous with [those of the Śruti], the consequence would be their sublation (bādha).
If it is argued that those [Smṛti texts] are general statements and that custom (ācāra) is weak, and therefore let there be sublation, we say no; as was illustrated in the example...

If [the term] were to have a meaning distinct from the scope of the verbal expression, there would be both the sublation of the established usage of the plural number and the necessity of postulating another underlying Vedic text (*śruti*). However, if it has the meaning as stated by us, there is neither sublation nor the need to postulate a *śruti*, because it is rooted in logic (*nyāya*). Furthermore, in the performance of the rites, there would be no sublation of the prescribed time for the *kutapa* cloth and so forth.

This follows as a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*). For if they were performed simultaneously, there would be a contradiction of those scriptural injunctions which prohibit the performance of another rite in the midst of one, such as: "While one [rite] is being performed, one should not perform various other rites.
Furthermore, the injunction regarding the performance (*prayoga-vidhi*) prohibits delay. Therefore, all [the constituent parts] must be performed [in succession].
The view favored by Viṣṇudharma is that [the subsidiaries] exist separately;
this is established when there is an absence of the apprehension of specific distinctions such as identity of place, time, and action.

As for the statement that the performance of the *prayāja* and other subsidiaries of sacrifices like the *Agniṣṭoma* is "tantra" (common/shared), that applies only to those subsidiaries which are grasped within a single performance-injunction (*ekaprayogavidhi*).

It is accumulated, but not in the independent *pradhāna* rites themselves. Furthermore, when the *nitya-apūrva* (eternal transcendental result) is pleased by the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices performed for the sake of a desired result (*kāmya*), that [result] is also appropriately [attributed] to the unity of the action.
And those very two collections, such as the *āgneya* and others, which exist for the sake of the *kāmya-apūrva*, are likewise produced for the sake of the *nitya-apūrva*.

Because their identity is understood from that single sentence; as for the conventional usage of difference therein, it is based on the distinction between the times of cognition caused by the connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as desire, form, and so forth, and not based on a real difference in the entity itself. However, the unprecedented difference is real due to the difference in qualification (*adhikāra*). Therefore, this [difference] is adventitious (*aupādhika*).

In the *Caturthacintāmayī*, within the *Pariśeṣa-saṃgraha* concerning the determination of time (*kāla-nirṇaya*), it was deliberated upon in the definition of difference (*bheda-lakṣaṇa*) whether [the result] is produced as a concomitant of the production of a distinct unprecedented entity (*apūrva-bheda-anuniṣpādaka*). Now, [one might ask]: "But..."

Furthermore, because the distinction between the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of the respective meanings of their original forms is understood, they are not identical due to the unity of the action.

Since the performance of the obligatory (nitya) rites is accomplished by the very same Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices performed for the sake of the optional (kāmya) apūrva, no separate performance is carried out; however, in the case of distinct actions, since the apūrva of one cannot be established by another, a separate performance is required for that purpose.

[The opponent claims: "There is a single performance [of all rites]. That is incorrect. Even when there is a difference between actions, because all actions are accomplished through their simultaneous performance at the same place, time, and agent, the production of all *apūrvas* (unseen potencies) occurs at one and the same time.
For at that moment, no distinction exists such as, "this is the completion of a specific [action]. This remains the case even when there is a difference in the ritual procedures (*thāga*).

Furthermore, because the deity is admitted to be present in the sovereignty of that *mānuṣāna* sacrifice; and likewise in the cases of crossing a river in a dream, being rained upon, and the recitation of mantras over impure things— wherein there is a simultaneous convergence of multiple causes characterized by the perception of various objects— the mantra-form consisting of the recitation of "The mind is poor, O wind" (*mano daridraṃ vātaḥ*) is bound to each individual cause.

It has been established in the Eleventh [Book] that when two *maitraka* [offerings] occur together, because there is no apprehension of a distinction, they are to be performed together (*sahomitikānuṣṭhāna*). Therefore, when there is a conjunction of occasions for *śrāddha*,
whether it be a conjunction of place, performer, or deity, because there is no apprehension of a distinction, it should be performed by way of a single performance (*tantra*).
The performance of all *śrāddhas*— namely, those occasioned by the lunar conjunction (*saṅghāta*), the new moon (*amāvāsyā*),
and the *vyatīpāta* yoga— one should perform these *śrāddhas* with the thought, "I shall do this for that purpose."
Thus concludes the determination regarding the Kāvya offerings.
Now follows the determination of the time for the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
In that regard, an inquiry is made concerning the cooking for the Vaiśvadeva, as it is relevant to that context: is it for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva and other rites?

Is the single act of cooking for the sake of the *māgñārtha* (the ancestral rite) one and the same, or is it distinct? In that regard, first, the cooking for the *nitya-māsa* (daily monthly rites), the *vaiśvadeva*, and so forth, contained within the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), is indeed one and the same; this is the view of Dhānyāyana.

Because the *pāka* (cooked food) performed daily is not for the sake of all rites such as *māneṣṭi* and so forth; and because during a period of impurity (*aśauca*),
prior to the eleventh day, there is no *vaiśvadeva* or similar rite at all, therefore at that time, by means of that [pāka], [one performs] the *navāśrāddhas*.

The Vaiśvadeva offering does not exist in the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite; rather, in the *śrāddha*s performed on the eleventh day (*aikādaśāhika*), the Vaiśvadeva is performed with a separate cooking. According to Devala’s statement, “In the *ekoddiṣṭa*, one should relinquish the entire remainder [of the food] to the Brahmins,” in those *ekoddiṣṭa*s known as *navaśrāddha*, all remnants of the food are indeed for the Brahmins.

Because of its specific injunction; furthermore, the use of *caitra* (sesame) will be mentioned in the context of *preta-śrāddhas*. Since the annual (*sāṃvatsara*) and other rites are modifications (*vikṛti*) of the New Moon (*amāvāsyā*) *śrāddha*, their determination follows the determination of the archetype (*prakṛti*). Thus, regarding the cooking for the New Moon *śrāddha*, there arises a doubt. In this regard, the teacher Karka [holds that] the *śrāddha* is performed from the cooking intended for the *vaiśvadeva* offering.

Having established the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "it must be performed," he stated the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that it should be done with the same cooking intended for the *vaiśvadeva* offering. The refutation of the reasons for that accepted prima facie view and its subsequent conclusion is set forth in the *Śrāddhakalpa*.

However, the teacher of ritual action (*karmopādhyāya*), being of our own school, has provided the reason for his own established conclusion: namely, because there is no mention of a separate cooking [for the ancestors].
It is criticized for being unestablished; one should perform the *pākayajña* for the sake of the ancestors and the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva* deities alone.
The *vaiśvadeva* is not for the sake of the ancestors, nor is the *darśa* sacrifice for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva*.

Because of these words of Saugāci, which state that the cooking is separate; for although here it might appear from the former [text] that one should prepare a single cooking for both purposes, nevertheless, according to the latter—namely, "the Vaiśvadeva is not for the ancestral rite"—no distinction in the cooking is made. The Vaiśvadeva...
Food cooked for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is indeed not for the purpose of the ancestors, nor for the Darśa-Śrāddha;

nor is it even for the purpose of the Nitya-Śrāddha. For there is a rule that the four daily rites—namely those dedicated to the Devas, Pitṛs, Bhūtas, and Manusyas—are accomplished by means of a single cooking.

Furthermore, the fortnight-long [period] for the sake of the Darśa-śrāddha does not serve the purpose of that very same deity; and by the word "Darśa," the procedures (itikartavyatā) of the Darśa-śrāddha— namely, the occasional (naimittika), optional (kāmya), and those ending with the Ekoddiṣṭa— are indicated.
In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, within the section on the determination of time (*Kālanirṇaya*) in the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa*,
it is stated that the *Śrāddhas* are indeed indicated by the term *Vaiśvadeva*, including the *Bhūtayajña*, *Pitṛyajña*, and *Manuṣyayajña*.

They are indeed perceived. But how can there be a suspicion regarding another purpose for that which is already considered to have a different purpose, especially since one does not admit the application of what has already been applied without a reason—even if it were by means of *adhihāna-lakṣaṇā* (indication through superimposition)? True;
however, it is not the case that here the fact of something having another purpose, while already existing as such, is being suspected or refuted; rather, [the point concerns] the *nirvāpa-pā-*...

The suspicion that there might be a single ritual procedure (*tantra*) for the two has been refuted; furthermore, even though it serves another purpose, it is introduced here as a relevant topic (*prasaṅga*).

This suspicion of relevance arises because, when actions performed at proximate times can be accomplished by a single procedure, there is an economy in the employment of the means of accomplishment. In this regard, [the text says]: "The Vaiśvadeva portion of the Darśa sacrifice is not [to be used here]. Regarding the sacrifice—
What was stated as a portion of the words of Garga should be understood to apply only when the Vaiśvadeva rite is performed before or during the Śrāddha, and not after it; for thus says Paiṭhīnasi:
He who performs the Vaiśvadeva rite after having set aside [a portion] from the food intended for the ancestors;

"That ancestral rite (*śrāddha*) would become demonic; it does not reach the ancestors. Now, one might object that the word "having extracted" (*uddhṛtya*) is redundant, because an oblation (*homa*) cannot be performed without having made a formal portioning (*avadāna*), and a portioning is simply the extraction of a single part from the whole. This is not so; for here, by the term "the cooked food of the ancestors" (*pitṛpāka*),...

The cooked substance (*pāka*) is designated as being in the state of having the ancestors (*pitṛ*) as its deity by virtue of being intended for them; from that state, the extraction of a portion is nothing other than the removal of that very deity-status, not merely a physical division. And this removal of the deity-status is only possible once the prior connection with the [previous] deity has been severed. Therefore, there is a removal from the ancestral deities.
Thus, this [act] is not established by the term "extraction" (*uddharaṇa*).

Furthermore, it is impossible to perform it either before or during the *śrāddha*, because it would subvert a specific mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*) of the form: "I shall prepare the cooked food intended for the ancestors at the time of extinguishing [the fire]. Nor is it possible to do so after it has been given, as [the fire] is... [mahipa-] (Note: The final fragment "mahipa-" appears to be a corrupted or incomplete portion of the source text.)
Once it has been set aside for that purpose, its subsequent removal is possible, because its status as dedicated to that deity has already been established.
For indeed, one cannot make something that is already established into something unestablished. But surely you do not say that what is established becomes unestablished?

It is not that [the substance] is produced; rather, it is said that it is consumed therein. Do not say so, because a cause of destruction is impossible.
If it is argued that the act of taking it out for the sake of another deity is the cause of destruction, we say no, because of its subsequent...
Because there is no evidence that [the new injunction] destroys the connection with the previous deity merely by being intent upon establishing a connection with a new deity;
for one might infer that it destroys the former [connection] because the subsequent connection cannot be established without the destruction of the previous one,
since two connections are contradictory in a single locus, and the cutting [of the connection] taught by the scriptural statement is the destroyer.

[The opponent says: "Not so. For being 'dedicated to that deity' (taddaivatyatva) consists precisely in being abandoned with reference to that deity; and that [status], having come into existence at the very moment of abandonment, perishes immediately thereafter. [The author replies: But in this way, [the status of being dedicated to a deity] applies even to an image or other substratum with reference to the presiding deity.

Furthermore, for that substance as well, its connection with the deity occurs only after the act of relinquishment and then perishes; consequently, since that substance has been accepted [by the deity], there would be no fault of stealing the property of a god in the event of its misappropriation. This is not so; for as for the substance that was relinquished for the purpose of being used in the worship of a permanent image and the like—

Because having that [deity] as its divinity results in the fruit of enjoyment, it does not perish as long as the enjoyment lasts; for if it were to perish, the persistence of the occasional effect would be difficult to establish once the cause has ceased. As for a substance whose enjoyment is completed, since the deity’s ownership there is mentioned merely as a secondary characteristic, let there be a prohibition against taking it, just as in the case of a *nirmālya* (an offering already used).

Therefore, after the *śrāddha*, the cooked food becomes connected with the ancestors; thus, one might think that by interrupting the sequence, one would destroy that connection. However, in reality, there is no connection with the ancestors in the remnants of the *śrāddha* at all;
rather, in the case of what remains after consumption, that connection has become merely indicative (*upalakṣaṇa*). And this [connection] does not persist in that state. [This is] the dancing.

Thus [ends the objection]. Now, why is it not explained that one should take a portion from the remainder of the *pitrya* cooking and divide it? It has already been stated that this is because [the word] *tuṅkṛtya* would be rendered meaningless. Therefore, whether the *pitrya* rite has not yet begun, or has begun but is not yet completed, for one who performs the *vaiśvadeva* by taking a portion from the cooking intended for the ancestors, [there is a fault].

The meaning of the statement is that such a *śrāddha* would become demonic (*āsura*). And this is logical: whatever is prepared for a specific purpose, if it is given to someone other than that intended recipient, then even if it is something mundane, it is considered defiled.

In the *Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa* of the *Catuḥśataka*, it is stated that even ordinary people consider such an act to be meritorious; how much more so when it is prepared for the sake of one’s parents or deities, let alone when it is being offered? When... [the text continues].

But when another [portion] is given from that same substance, no one at that time considers it to be either spoiled or improper. Furthermore, it has been stated that after the *śrāddha* ceremony, the materials used for the *śrāddha* may also be employed in the *vaiśvadeva* rite.
Thus says Paiṭhīnasi:
"Having performed the *śrāddha* according to the rules, one should then perform the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites; thereafter,
one should likewise give alms and so forth."

Here, by the word *ataḥ* (therefore), the meaning of the preceding verse is stated as the reason. By the second [word], it is said: "from the food remaining from the *śrāddha*. Therefore, the meaning is this: since if the *vaiśvadeva* were performed with the food prepared for the ancestors (*pitṛpāka*) before the *śrāddha*, that *śrāddha* would become *āsura* (demonic), therefore—

The meaning is that after having performed the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha, one should then take a portion from what remains of that śrāddha and perform the Vaiśvadeva and other rites. Nor should it be argued that because the food (*anna*) has not been previously mentioned, it is unfit to be referred to by the pronoun "that" (*tat*); for in the previously cited statement, "having drawn [the portion] from the food cooked for the ancestors," there is a continuous thematic progression (*prakrama*) regarding the food.
And by the word "all" (sarva), the assembly is referred to. Nor is there a rule that proximity [of meaning] depends solely on physical juxtaposition;
for it is accepted that proximity consists in being present in the intellect. Here, by the word "etc.
(ādi), the daily obligatory rite (nityaka-karma) accomplished by all mantras is included; therefore, the obligatory Śrāddha is also [included] among the Śrāddhas.

It should not be performed from the remnants of the cooking. Thus, if one performs the Vaiśvadeva at the conclusion of the dismissal of the Brāhmaṇas, then it is with the very same cooking intended for the Śrāddha; but if one performs the Vaiśvadeva at any one of the three times prior to the dismissal of the Brāhmaṇas in the manner to be described, then [it should be done] separately.

Regarding the phrase "by means of compassion" (*kṛpānena*): here, the author of the *Smṛticandrikā*, having cited the statement of Laugākṣi—"One should offer for the sake of the father [using] *yavāgū*, etc.; the *vaiśvadeva* offering is not for the inheritance"—explains that the meaning of the word is intended for the purpose of the *darśaśrāddha*.

Even when a *śrāddha* is performed with a measured amount [of food], it does not serve the purpose of the *vaiśvadeva* offering; having explained this and stated that it concerns the *agnimukha-śrāddha*, he further stated the underlying logic: for one who possesses [the full measure]...

Because the Vaiśvadeva rite must be performed by the prescribed rule even prior to the Darśa-śrāddha, as it cannot be joined with the Śrāddha due to its being a cooked offering (pakva-haviṣka). This very principle establishes a meaning that is precisely the opposite of what was intended;
for if the Vaiśvadeva were absent at a later time, the injunction would be untenable, as there would be no remnant of the Śrāddha to serve as the material for the prasūti offering.
If it is argued that this prohibition pertains only to the earlier time, then it would apply only to the cases involving both those with fires (*sāgnika*) and those without fires (*anagnika*).

Alternatively, if it is said that even though the status of being a prohibitive injunction is untenable because the action is already established, it might still be a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*), then two defects would be incurred: namely, its status as a mere restatement and its resulting pointlessness (*ānarthakya*).

Moreover, there is indeed a disparity here: since the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice becomes the locus for both the earlier and later times, the prohibitive injunction applies to the earlier time, while it is a restatement of a prohibition regarding the later time. Therefore, [the rule applies] to the times prior to the dismissal of the Brāhmaṇas.

Let the scriptural statement prohibiting the unification of the cooking for the *cit* Vaiśvadeva with that for the Śrāddha apply specifically to the cases of those who maintain the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) and those who do not (*anagnika*). As for the view held by some regarding such texts as, “Having performed the Śrāddha according to the rule, one should thereafter perform the Vaiśvadeva and other rites,” which prescribe the performance of the Vaiśvadeva and so forth with the remnants of the Śrāddha—

The placement of these statements is within the annual and other Śrāddhas that are modifications (*vikṛti*) of the Darśa-Śrāddha; as for the rule "the Vaiśvadevika portion is not for the sake of the [ancestors]," its placement is in the Darśa-Śrāddha alone—this is how it should be understood: all these general injunctions commence specifically with the Darśa-Śrāddha.

There is no such thing as an unattached statement (*anārabhyavāda*) anywhere; or even if it were to exist, nevertheless, by the principle that "it belongs to the archetype because it is spread out [therein]," just as in the case of the rule "the sacrificial ladle is made of *parṇa* wood," its placement is restricted to the *darśa-śrāddha* due to the absence of a restrictive rule. Now, if it be argued that it is studied as an unattached statement—

Since the injunction of an *anārabhyavāda* (unattached statement) finds its place within the *prakṛti* (archetype) that is encompassed by the *dharma*, therein, because the previously performed action is determined by the context and because there is no contradiction with what is studied as unattached (*anārabhyādhīta*), therefore—
In the *Caturaṅgacintāmaṇi*, within the section on the determination of the *bāla* (the remaining portion), [Folio 11a].
It should not be said that this rule does not apply to the *darśa-śrāddha*.

one should then, immediately thereafter, offer that portion of food set aside for the *śrāddha* to them— that is, to those who are eligible for the *śrāddha*— first, before [the main offering]. One should give it.

Now, the determination of the time for the Vaiśvadeva according to the primary context is being made.

The necessity of performing the cooking is indeed established;

If the *prativārika* (the one who guards against obstacles) is appointed at the beginning of the śrāddha and other rites, [he must be maintained].
"The gods do not accept the *havya* offerings, nor do the ancestors accept the *kavya* offerings"— this is the prohibition established by Gautama.
"But he who performs the *vaiśvadeva* rite without having first performed the *śrāddha*..."
"That śrāddha remains present for the ancestors.

"The remainder of the two worldly fires remains for the ancestors.

That does not mean that one should perform the *vaiśvadeva* rite after the *śrāddha*, having set aside [a portion] from the *śrāddha* cooking.

This prohibits *nasya* (the offering of the first portion). The Vaiśvadeva oblation prior to the Śrāddha has not been prohibited by anyone; therefore, it should indeed be performed. It is replied: since the Vaiśvadeva is prescribed to be performed after the Śrāddha with the remnants of the Śrāddha, there is a prohibition against performing it with a portion produced from the Śrāddha cooking itself; [this applies] at that specific time, and not at other times.

The subject matter [of the rule] regarding the *vaiśvadeva* performed prior to the *śrāddha* has been explained; likewise, those [rules] concerning other times—namely, that it is strictly prohibited [at those times]—must also be explained. Thus, one who does not maintain a sacred fire (*anagnika*) should perform the *vaiśvadeva* even with the food prepared for the *śrāddha* during the time preceding the *śrāddha*, but not in the midst of the *śrāddha* itself.
Sometimes it may be by means of cooking on a Śaṅku (a wooden pin), but only after the cooking process has begun; however, prior to the Śrāddha, it is in every way forbidden.

"It must indeed be performed. Now, if all the prohibitions regarding what ought to be done refer to the Vaiśvadeva rite occurring within the Śrāddha, whether they share that same single subject matter or have distinct subjects, there would be a threefold restriction (*saṅkoca*).

It does not [apply]. For instance, the general agent—which is implied by the action, indicated by the number expressed by the verbal suffix, or denoted by the verbal suffix itself—is a universal agent that pervades both specific types of agents, namely those possessing fire (*sāgnika*) and those lacking fire (*anagnika*).
This universal agent is restricted to a single particular case, namely the one who lacks fire, in the case of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, which has an agent who possesses fire.

The exclusion of the agent [of the Vaiśvadeva] is because, by the rule of its non-existence at the prior time, it lacks existence at the intermediate time. For the general form of the Vaiśvadeva action—

which is understood from the word *vaiśvadeva* alone, which pervades multiple individual Vaiśvadeva actions occurring at the prior and intermediate times— would, if restricted to the single object of the intermediate-time Vaiśvadeva action, result in a contradiction regarding the action.

[[page 971-to-971]] [[page 972-to-972]] [[page 973-to-973]] *The Great Treatise on the Stages of the Path to Enlightenment: The Chapter on the Perfection of Wisdom* By Je Tsongkhapa Lobzang Drakpa **Chapter Four: The Perfection of Wisdom** **Section One: The Superiority of the Perfection of Wisdom** **Subsection One: The Superiority of the Perfection of Wisdom in Terms of Its Nature** The perfection of wisdom is superior to the other perfections because it is the mother of all the buddhas and bodhisattvas. As it is said: "The Buddhas of the three times, having relied upon this very perfection of wisdom, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, it is the antidote to the ignorance that obscures the nature of reality; it is the eye that perceives the ultimate truth, and it is the supreme medicine that cures the disease of all afflictive and cognitive obscurations. **Subsection Two: The Superiority of the Perfection of Wisdom in Terms of Its Function** In terms of its function, the perfection of wisdom is superior because it brings about the attainment of the two types of omniscience—the knowledge of all aspects and the knowledge of the paths—and it establishes one in the state of a buddha. It is through the power of wisdom that the bodhisattva practices the six perfections without attachment, dedicating them toward the welfare of all sentient beings. Without wisdom, the other five perfections are like a blind person without a guide; they cannot lead one to the city of liberation. However, when conjoined with wisdom, they become the path to enlightenment. **Subsection Three:

The Superiority of the Perfection of Wisdom in Terms of Its Result** Regarding its result, the perfection of wisdom is superior because it results in the attainment of the dharmakāya, the body of ultimate reality, which is the source of all the qualities of a buddha. It is the cause for the manifestation of the rūpakāyas (form bodies) that appear to disciples in various ways to benefit them. Thus, the perfection of wisdom is the most essential of all the perfections. **Subsection Four: How to Practice the Perfection of Wisdom** To practice the perfection of wisdom, one must first understand the two truths: conventional truth and ultimate truth. Conventional truth refers to the world of appearances as perceived by ordinary beings, while ultimate truth is the emptiness of inherent existence of those very appearances. One should cultivate the wisdom that realizes that all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, yet understand that this emptiness does not negate the dependent arising of conventional phenomena. This non-dual realization of appearance and emptiness is the essence of the perfection of wisdom. One should train in this by relying on the instructions of a qualified spiritual mentor, studying the authentic scriptures, and engaging in analytical meditation to gain certainty in the meaning of emptiness. Through the union of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and special insight (*vipaśyanā*), one should gradually eliminate the misconceptions regarding the nature of self and phenomena until the direct realization of emptiness is attained. **Subsection Five: The Obstacles to the Perfection of Wisdom and Their Antidotes** The primary obstacles to the perfection of wisdom are the four types of grasping at true existence: grasping at the self of persons, grasping at the self of phenomena, grasping at the extremes of eternalism and nihilism, and grasping at the characteristics of things. The antidotes to these are the four immeasurables, the four applications of mindfulness, the correct elimination of the four distortions, and the cultivation of the view of the middle way, respectively. By applying these antidotes, one overcomes the afflictions and the conceptual obscurations that hinder the realization of wisdom. **Subsection Six: The Benefits of Cultivating the Perfection of Wisdom** The benefits of cultivating the perfection of wisdom are immeasurable. In this life, it increases one's intelligence, memory, and eloquence, and it protects one from all harm. In future lives, it leads to rebirth in higher realms and eventually to the attainment of buddhahood. Moreover, it ensures that one’s roots of virtue are inexhaustible and that one’s merit grows infinitely. Therefore, one should strive to practice the perfection of wisdom with great diligence. *** **Chapter Five: The Perfection of Skillful Means** **Section One: The Superiority of Skillful Means** Skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) is the ability to apply the teachings in a way that effectively benefits others and leads them to liberation. It is superior because it ensures that the practice of the perfections is not wasted and that one’s own realization matures into the benefit of others. Without skillful means, even if one attains a high level of meditative concentration, one may fall into the extreme of peace and fail to turn toward the welfare of sentient beings. With skillful means, however, one can manifest in various forms to guide others according to their individual needs and capacities. **Section Two: The Types of Skillful Means** There are many types of skillful means, including: the means of gathering disciples through the four methods of attraction;

the means of transforming the mind through the four immeasurables; the means of ripening sentient beings through the six perfections; and the means of entering the path through the three gates of liberation. Among these, the most fundamental is the ability to distinguish between what is beneficial and what is harmful for each individual, and to act accordingly. **Section Three: How to Practice Skillful Means** To practice skillful means, one must first develop a vast accumulation of merit through generosity, ethical discipline, and patience. Then, one must cultivate the wisdom that understands the nature of reality. With these two—merit and wisdom—one can employ various methods to lead others to the Dharma. This involves using worldly activities such as medicine, arts, and crafts to create opportunities for teaching, as well as employing the profound methods of the Mahāyāna to inspire others to generate the bodhicitta. **Section Four: The Obstacles to Skillful Means and Their Antidotes** The main obstacles to skillful means are attachment to one’s own comfort, a lack of compassion for others, and a narrow-minded view of the Dharma. The antidotes are the cultivation of great compassion, the dedication of all roots of virtue to the welfare of others, and the study of the vast range of teachings in the Mahāyāna sūtras and tantras to broaden one’s perspective. **Section Five: The Benefits of Skillful Means** The benefits of skillful means are that it allows the bodhisattva to remain in saṃsāra voluntarily to help others, without being bound by its defects. It ensures that the bodhisattva’s practice is never in vain and that every action contributes to the attainment of buddhahood. Ultimately, it is the bridge that connects the practitioner’s own realization with the liberation of all sentient beings. *** **Chapter Six: The Perfection of Vow** **Section One: The Superiority of the Perfection of Vow** The perfection of vow (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) is the power of aspiration that directs all one’s actions toward the attainment of enlightenment for the sake of all beings. It is superior because it provides the momentum that carries the bodhisattva across the vast ocean of saṃsāra. Without the power of vow, even if one has the intention to help others, one may lack the persistence to do so over the long term. With vow, one remains committed to the goal regardless of difficulties. **Section Two: The Nature of Vow** Vow is characterized by a firm determination and an unwavering resolve. It is not merely a wish, but a commitment backed by the power of previous roots of virtue. There are two main types of vow: the vow to attain enlightenment oneself and the vow to liberate all sentient beings. These vows are further divided into general vows and specific vows, such as the ten great vows of Samantabhadra. **Section Three: How to Generate Vow** To generate vow, one should reflect deeply on the suffering of all sentient beings and the rarity of the opportunity to practice the Dharma. One should then cultivate the bodhicitta and make a formal commitment to follow the bodhisattva path. This can be done through the ritual of taking the bodhisattva vows, which involves generating the aspiration and the application bodhicitta. Once the vow is taken, one must maintain it through constant mindfulness and vigilance. **Section Four: The Obstacles to Vow and Their Antidotes** The obstacles to vow include forgetfulness, laziness, and a lack of enthusiasm for the Dharma. The antidotes are the cultivation of mindfulness and introspective awareness, the practice of joyous effort (*vīrya*), and the recollection of the benefits of the bodhisattva path. One should also rely on the power of confession and the power of restoration whenever the vow is impaired. **Section Five: The Benefits of Vow** The benefits of vow are that it acts as a seal that binds all one’s actions to the path of enlightenment. It prevents one from falling back into the lower realms and ensures that one’s merits increase exponentially. Most importantly, it guarantees that one will never abandon the practice of the Dharma, even in the face of great adversity. *** **Chapter Seven:
